articles.title_orig: Stock futures rise as chip stocks gain for a second day, oil prices ease: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures rise as chip stocks gain for a second day, oil prices ease: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices ticked lower Tuesday driven by a diplomatic push to de-escalate tensions between Saudi Arabia and Iran.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, were down 77 cents to $115.04 a barrel as of 8:55 a.m. ET. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were 70 cents lower to $101.06 a barrel.
Saudi Arabia's defense minister and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian held direct talks in Tehran on Monday. Senior military and intelligence officials from Pakistan and Turkey, who are allied with the Saudis, also participated.
Saudi Arabia has come under repeated attack from Iran-allied Houthi militants in recent weeks. The Houthis have bombed energy infrastucture as well as civilian targets such as airports.
The Houthi strikes threaten to disrupt Saudi oil exports, which have proven resilient during eight months of conflict in the region.
Iran's Foreign Minister Esmaeil Baqaei said the talks in Tehran were a step toward regional security cooperation and further consultations are possible, according to the state media outlet Tasnim .
The diplomatic push comes as U.S. President Donald Trump said in an interview with Fox News on Sunday that he was approaching a decision on whether to strike a deal with Iran or intensify military operations, suggesting that additional attacks remained an option.
Representatives from Qatar, which has helped mediate negotiations between Washington and Tehran, also traveled to the Iranian capital on Sunday, Reuters reported .
Prospects of a diplomatic breakthrough have helped temper fears of further disruptions to global energy supplies, putting downward pressure on crude prices.
But earlier oil price losses were limited as the prospect of a lasting resolution appeared fragile, with Iran-backed Houthi militants continuing their attacks on Saudi Arabia over the weekend.
—CNBC's Justina Lee contributed to the report.

articles.title_orig: Boeing Stock Rises After the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Earnings Quarter
articles.title_zh: Boeing Stock Rises After the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Earnings Quarter
articles.content_orig:
Boeing narrowed its loss in the third quarter after defense sales rose, but CEO Kelly Ortberg told staff that the manufacturer has "more work to do."
Here's what Boeing reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:
For the three months ended Sept. 30, Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss, or $7.14 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, the company posted a loss of 34 cents a share. A year earlier, Boeing had taken a nearly $5 billion charge on its long-delayed 777X aircraft program.
Revenue climbed 4% on the year to $24.19 billion. Free cash flow rose to $464 million from $238 million in the third quarter of 2025.
The company's defense unit revenue jumped 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.94 billion.
Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the third quarter, one more jet than a year earlier.
Revenue in the all-important commercial aircraft business fell 3% to $10.72 billion. The unit had a negative operating margin of 6.5% because of a "less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs," Boeing said.
The plane manufacturer's executives are set to update investors on how quickly it can increase aircraft production in the coming months when it holds a quarterly earnings call on Tuesday at 10:30 a.m. ET.
Boeing has been producing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month, but is aiming for more. Ortberg told investors last month that production is taking "a little bit longer" than expected to stabilize, and the company expects to increase its output of the planes next year.
"Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday. "That means elevating our performance through lean, productivity and efficiency improvements in our day-to-day work while upholding our high levels of safety and quality."
Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it.
But the manufacturer had some wins lately. The U.S. Navy tapped Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet.
And the Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the 737 Max 10 , the largest in the Max family. That followed the approval of the 737 Max 7 in August and marked the final certifications for the aircraft line.

articles.title_orig: Intel to Buy Quantum Startup Classiq for About $2.3 Billion
articles.title_zh: Intel to Buy Quantum Startup Classiq for About $2.3 Billion
articles.content_orig:
The deal, expected to close in the first half of 2027 pending regulatory approvals, would add quantum processors to Intel's chip lineup
Justin Sullivan / Getty Images
Intel $INTC agreed to acquire Classiq , an Israeli quantum computing software company, in a deal expected to close in the first half of 2027, the company said.
The transaction is subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions. Until it closes, Intel and Classiq will operate as separate, independent companies. Intel announced the agreement on Monday.
Intel 's announcement did not include a price. The chipmaker will pay roughly $2.3 billion, according to Bloomberg .
Intel said the deal would combine Classiq's platform for automated quantum algorithm synthesis with Intel 's quantum software, silicon spin-qubit technology and chip manufacturing expertise. Intel said the combination would make it a full-stack quantum solutions provider and let it add quantum processing units, or QPUs, to a portfolio that spans CPUs, GPUs and application-specific integrated circuits.
"Joining forces with Classiq transforms Intel 's Quantum Computing Group into a full-stack quantum computing business," Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said in a statement, according to Bloomberg.
Intel has invested in quantum computing development since 2015, the company said. After the deal closes, Intel intends to continue supporting Classiq's existing integrations across multiple platforms and to keep the software independent of the underlying qubit type and hardware.
"Together, Intel and Classiq can help unlock the benefits of quantum computing and accelerate its adoption sooner," Nir Minerbi, Classiq's co-founder and CEO, said in a statement.
Classiq's customers include BMW AG and AT&T $T Inc., according to Bloomberg. According to Bloomberg, the startup, which employs roughly 130 people, has brought in over $200 million in funding.
Other large technology companies are moving quantum hardware toward use alongside classical processors in data centers . Microsoft $MSFT has been pushing a quantum processor designed to fit into standard server rack footprints, and IBM $IBM has a quantum computer running next to a classical supercomputer.

articles.title_orig: China’s Hengrui posts 89% rise in third-quarter net profit, beating estimates
articles.title_zh: China’s Hengrui posts 89% rise in third-quarter net profit, beating estimates
articles.content_orig:
Net profit reached 2.46 billion yuan for the quarter, also above analyst estimates
Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals, one of China’s largest drug makers, reported a 20.55 per cent rise in third-quarter revenue to 8.95 billion yuan (US$1.34 billion), beating analyst estimates of 8.55 billion yuan amid stronger innovative drug sales.
Net profit reached 2.46 billion yuan for the three months ended September 30, jumping 88.92 per cent year on year and exceeding the Bloomberg analyst consensus estimate of 2.38 billion yuan.
Improving innovative drug sales and out-licensing revenue contributed to the growth, the company said in a Tuesday filing.

articles.title_orig: China’s economy may never overtake America — and it’s all due to an ill-fated 47-year-old policy
articles.title_zh: China’s economy may never overtake America — and it’s all due to an ill-fated 47-year-old policy
articles.content_orig:
Just one child doomed China’s hopes of overtaking the US.
The Middle Kingdom, once a surging economic growth engine expected to eclipse the US economy in just a few years, is not expected to outgrow the US until the 2040s now — if it does at all.
And it’s largely down to China’s 1979 One Child Policy , which is devastating growth, according to Yi Fuxian, a Chinese demographer at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.
Plummeting birth rates and economic problems have erased the 6+% per year growth that China reported before the COVID-19 pandemic.
Many economists in both China and the West were taken in by the Chinese Communist Party’s inflated official figures, which massively overestimated the country’s consumer power, Fuxian said.
It comes as a Goldman Sachs study found that China’s population began shrinking in 2022 , just 13 years after that of neighboring Japan. And its decline is on track to be far steeper, dramatically damaging the country’s economic prospects, the Financial Times reported .
China has a GDP of $21.6 trillion — just two-thirds the size of the US economy.
Yi told The Post that official Chinese statistics have systematically inflated the country’s birthrates and total population figures going back decades.
While official reports claim China has a population of over 1.4 billion, Yi calculates that the true figure in 2020 was “under 1.28 billion,” at least 130 million lower than reported.
India actually surpassed China as the world’s most populous nation years earlier than officially recognized, according to Yi, author of the 2007 book, “Big Country with an Empty Nest,” which criticized China’s one-child policies.
The US, the third most populous country in the world, has 342 million people — about a quarter the population of China.
Yi argues that China’s population actually began shrinking in 2018, four years earlier than Goldman Sachs’ estimate, and more than a decade before the official projection of 2031 to 2034.
Most of this can be attributed to China’s notorious One Child Policy , instituted to limit Chinese families to one child per mother, over fears of spiraling population growth and widespread poverty.
While the policy was relaxed to two children per couple in 2016 and three children in 2021, China’s total fertility rate remains one of the lowest in the world .
China is no longer poor — officially 0% of the population is in extreme poverty, compared to 88% 40 years ago.
But it’s also not rich; the per capita GDP is about $13,800 per year, about 15% of that in the US.
Turkey, Russia and Kazakhstan are all richer than China by that measure.
The country’s total fertility rate fell below the 2.1 replacement level in 1991 and continued to plummet, dropping below 1.0 and now estimated to be just 0.8 births per woman, according to Yi.
Last year saw a record low of just 8 million live births in China. The much smaller US, by contrast, had 3.6 million births.
Yi also blames the economic reforms of China’s former Premier Zhu Rongji in the 1990s, for causing “many problems” that slowed down China’s economic growth and race to catch up with the US.
Decades of strict birth restrictions and fiscal centralization severely curtailed household disposable income in China, to roughly 42-44% of GDP.
In contrast, in the US, that figure is over 70% of GDP.
While this may have helped China’s economy in the short term, allowing it to flood the US with cheap imported goods, in the long run, it may have signed the CCP’s suicide note, according to Yi.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
Children function as “super-consumers,” driving much of household spending, he explained.
With China missing several full generations worth of children, this severely crippled Chinese domestic consumption, he argued.
To offset weak domestic consumption, China became heavily dependent on manufacturing exports, an unsustainable real estate bubble, and state-subsidized industrial overcapacity, he explained.
Those policies, “killed China’s economy, the population and the economy — and also killed America’s manufacturing,” Yi said.
China is now one of the oldest countries in the world, with a rapidly shrinking labor pool and aging population. The median age is expected to reach 59 by 2050, compared to 44 in the US.
This means Beijing may never catch up with the US economically — and worse, could face a long-term economic deceleration, Yi argued.
Yi puts the over-optimistic predictions about China’s economic growth down to mainstream economists and Chinese government-aligned institutions relying on fabricated data — assuming China’s population would soon grow five times larger than the US.
This played into the popular narrative that “the East is rising while the West is declining,” he said, while the truth is very different.
“By 2029 to 2035, China will lag behind the US across all major demographic and growth metrics,” Yi said.
However, for pro-democracy activists who might hope that this demographic time bomb could topple the CCP, Yi has a warning.
Contrary to Western expectations that economic development would foster a pro-democracy middle class, China’s rapid aging has depleted it of the young population required to drive political activism.
Just 16% of China is aged 15 to 29, down from 31% at the time of China’s last mass-democracy movement in 1989, which culminated in the communists’ brutal crackdown in Tiananmen Square.
An aging, risk-averse China is far more likely to support a centralized strongman who will safeguard pensions and social stability, Yi explained.

articles.title_orig: SoFi Reports Third Quarter 2026 with Record Net Revenue of $1.4 Billion, Net Income of $241 Million and Raises Full-Year Guidance
articles.title_zh: SoFi Reports Third Quarter 2026 with Record Net Revenue of $1.4 Billion, Net Income of $241 Million and Raises Full-Year Guidance
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Third quarter earnings season is in full swing this week, with corporate results on deck from Big Tech heavy-hitters Microsoft ( MSFT ), Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Amazon ( AMZN ).
Aside from Big Tech, industries from oil to chips to pharmaceuticals will be represented, as Exxon Mobil ( XOM ), Intel ( INTC ), Boeing ( BA ), Ford ( F ), and Eli Lilly ( LLY ) also open their books.
It's shaping up to be another strong earnings season. According to FactSet data , nearly a quarter of S&P 500 companies have already reported Q3 earnings so far, with an overall earnings growth rate of 29.5%. If that rate holds, it will mark the third straight quarter of earnings growth above 25%.
SoFi ( SOFI ) stock surged 10% in premarket trading on Tuesday after the online financial services provider lifted its 2026 outlook and reported strong results for the third quarter.
Here's what SoFi reported for Q3, compared to Wall Street analyst estimates compiled by S&P Market Intelligence:
Revenue: up 45.9% year over year to $1.39 billion, above estimates of $1.26 billion.
Adjusted earnings: $0.18, above estimates of $0.17.
Updated 2026 guidance: SoFi now expects net revenue of $5.04 billion in 2026, reflecting a 40% year-over-year increase. Adjusted EBITDA is now expected at $1.66 billion of adjusted EBITDA, and earnings per share are forecast at $0.61. Wall Street analysts were expecting 2026 earnings per share of $0.59.
The company also introduced 2027 guidance, guiding for $0.90 of earnings per share, which is above the Street's estimate of $ 0.82.
"We had exceptional Q3 results against the backdrop of any environment, but they are even more remarkable given how 2026 has unfolded," CEO Anthony Noto said. "Our focus is simple. We are adding more members, who are using more products, and generating more revenue per product to create the most value for our shareholders over the long run. In less than a decade, we have transformed SoFi from a single-product company into an everything financial app with eight different businesses each generating over $100 million in annualized revenue."
Whirlpool posted another mixed quarter as inflation and lower demand in North America took a toll.
"What is new and different is the increasingly inflationary environment that has happened from Q2 into Q3, as well as the impact of volume deleveraging which is driven by the softer demand that we have in the North America industry," Whirlpool CFO Roxanne Warner told Yahoo Finance, adding that the team is focusing on what it can control.
In the third quarter, the company reported revenue declined by nearly 9% to $3.68 billion, which was below estimates of $3.91 billion. The company reported an adjusted loss per share of $0.21, lower than the adjusted earnings per share estimate of $0.76,  per Bloomberg consensus data
Warner said that the industry hasn't caught up to the "full impact of the inflationary pressures from 2022," with inflation up 12% since then.
For that reason,  the company plans to raise prices for the third time this year, now by 7% in the fourth quarter. That follows its largest price increase in history in April, at 10%, and a 4% increase in its list prices in July.
Revenue for major appliances in its North America business fell 8.3% year over year to $2.5 billion, below Wall Street's expectations.
Whirlpool's small domestic appliance business fell almost 1% to $286 million, below the expected $314 million. However, the company said that in the third quarter, some items sold out, leading to roughly 40% year-over-year growth in US orders in October.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: 8-month Iran war looms over Israeli election as Egypt wades into Saudi's fight with the Houthis
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: 8-month Iran war looms over Israeli election as Egypt wades into Saudi's fight with the Houthis
articles.content_orig:
What to know about the Iran war:
An oil slick in the Gulf has reached a beach in the United Arab Emirates, video from the AFP news agency showed on Tuesday, with experts warning it could threaten desalination plants as it spreads.
UAE authorities said Friday that they had "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," referring to an emirate north of Dubai.
By Tuesday morning, footage shot by AFP showed workers cleaning up oil on the emirate's beaches, which had been shut earlier by authorities along with other beaches in the country.
Satellite images taken on Oct. 21 and analyzed by AFP show what appears to be a slick of about 70 square miles in that area. Three days later, images showed it had quadrupled in size to around 290 square miles.
Experts from NGOs including Dutch peace group PAX said oil came from the tanker GEM NO.2 after it was attacked on Oct. 9.
They warned the slick could affect operations at UAE desalination plants, crucial for supplying water to the Gulf country.
"Satellite imagery from October 26 shows oil slicks a few hundred metres away from the intake of the Naqaa desalination plant. It remains unclear to what extent this will affect the process at the plant itself,"  said Wim Zwijnenburg from PAX.
The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on Oct. 9 that a vessel had been hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control.
Mohsen Rezaee, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said regional countries should not rely on the United States for security, arguing that Washington has failed to provide credible security guarantees.
In a post on X Tuesday, Rezaee wrote: "America has not brought security to any country in the region, and Washington's inability to provide security guarantees has become clear. Security in West Asia must originate from within the region, and any foreign intervention must be prevented."
The U.S. has military bases in several Gulf countries that repeatedly were targeted at the height of the war.
A Houthi official said Tuesday that the Egyptian parliament's decision to authorize President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to deploy forces to Saudi Arabia to help the kingdom defend against the Iran-backed group's attacks was a declaration of war.
"Egypt and its parliament declared support for what is called the defense of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and in doing so, it declares war against the Republic of Yemen," said Mohammed Ali al-Houthi, a member of the Houthi political bureau, in a Telegram post.
El-Sisi stressed last week that the Egyptian deployment would be entirely defensive, "and does not include an attack on Yemen."
Oil prices held more or less steady early Tuesday, with international benchmark Brent crude hovering around $116 a barrel, little changed from the previous day when senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting. Tehran said the discussions were "very good."
Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis," a Saudi foreign ministry statement said.
The talks followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war, with some observers suggesting the period between next Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections and the new Congress taking office could be particularly fraught.
Also in view are elections in Israel, where voters began delivering their verdict on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who told President Trump a week ago that they have "a job to finish" in Iran.
Israelis started casting votes Tuesday morning in a national election set to shape the country's next government , with the Iran war looming large over their decisions.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, echoing warnings issued repeatedly by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for weeks leading up to the vote, told voters that they were facing a decision "between two security paradigms: an approach based on offense, initiative, and decisive victory — or a return to a policy of containment and restraint."
"We have struck Iran twice and eliminated existential threats; we have expanded Israel's security perimeter in Lebanon, Syria, and Gaza to protect Israeli communities; and we are currently strengthening and fortifying our eastern border and the Jordan Valley," he said, calling on Israeli voters to "support this path in order to finish the job."
Netanyahu has called for Israel and the U.S. to resume attacks on Iran, telling President Trump , who has endorsed him enthusiastically, last week, "we have a job to finish."
The Iranian regime has dismissed the importance of the Israeli election, with foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei telling reporters Monday that the outcome will have no bearing on Iran's preparedness to face a resumption of hostilities, or to negotiate a deal to end the war based on its longstanding demands.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthi rebels said on Tuesday that it had shot down three missiles fired by the group toward the kingdom's eastern region.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Eastern Province," coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki wrote on X.
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran on Monday in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting, with Tehran saying the discussions were "very good."
Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis," a Saudi foreign ministry statement said. It was the first joint visit to Tehran by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey since they formed a defense alliance in Mecca, the holy city in western Saudi Arabia, in August.
The talks, which included heavyweight Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war.
The delegations met Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. The meeting ended without concrete announcements, with the various parties saying they "agreed to continue discussions" according to Iranian state media.
But Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said the discussions in the capital were "very good," according to state television. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen," said the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
He said they agreed that security in the region "should be achieved by the countries themselves, and that we must prevent any kind of foreign intervention," saying emphasis was put on the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon, southern Syria, Gaza and the West Bank.
Kuwait condemned three men to death on Monday for plotting the assassination of the deputy prime minister, collaborating with Iran and joining Hezbollah, two judiciary sources told AFP.
The three men are all from the Shia Muslim community, which makes up around a third of Kuwait's population.
Huseein Abdallah al-Maatouq, a religious dignitary and secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, was among the three condemned by the criminal court, the sources said.
Another of the trio had been convicted in 2016 of terrorism before being pardoned by the country's emir. He was arrested again in April, the sources said.
The men are accused of undermining national interests, collaborating with Iran, planning the assassination of the deputy prime minister and interior minister, and membership of Hezbollah, which is classified as a terrorist group by Kuwait.
The court sentenced 11 other people connected to the case to five years of hard labor.

articles.title_orig: Finland and Norway Hold ‘Frank’ Call With Putin on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Finland and Norway Hold ‘Frank’ Call With Putin on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
The leaders of Finland and Norway called Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to urge him to end the war in Ukraine , breaking with a longstanding practice among Western European leaders of shunning direct contact with the Kremlin.
The phone call by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere was a bid to influence the diplomatic process at a time when President Donald Trump has shifted his position in favor of Russia and U.S. ties with Ukraine have hit their lowest point in 18 months.
The Nordic leaders spoke by phone to Putin and afterward to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, according to a Zelenskyy aide.
“The discussion (with Putin) was frank and substantive. We are neighboring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions,” Stubb said in a joint statement with Stoere.
The Norwegian added: “The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation.”
Both leaders stressed their strong support for Ukraine, which they said would continue.
The Kremlin’s readout of the call did not suggest that Putin had signaled any compromise from previously stated positions.
“It was emphasized that achieving a just and long-term peace is possible only if the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation are fully and unconditionally taken into account,” the Kremlin said.
“At the same time, attention was drawn to the confrontational policies of EU and NATO countries, which are contributing to the prolongation of the hostilities.”
Western European leaders have mostly shunned contact with Putin, while piling up sanctions on Moscow, since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022.
But that stance has left them sidelined as efforts to end the war have been led by Trump, who is seen in many EU capitals as unpredictable, erratic and prone to side with Putin at the expense of Ukraine.
That perception has been reinforced by deals this month in which Putin agreed to supply Russian diesel to the US and Trump eased sanctions on Russia while saying it was time for Ukrainians to replace Zelenskyy as their leader. Ukraine has also complained of disruption to intelligence-sharing by the US and to satellite internet services on which its military relies.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized the Finnish-Norwegian decision to talk to Putin, adding that she saw no signs that Russia wants peace.
“I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo,” Frederiksen told public broadcaster DR.
Stubb and Stoere participated in the call as leaders of their respective countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe as a whole, they said, adding that the two Nordic nations will continue their longstanding support for Ukraine.
Russia has frequently accused European governments of stoking the war by arming Ukraine and refusing direct talks.
It has contrasted the stance of Western European leaders with that of Trump, who has engaged with Putin and tried — so far without success — to broker a peace agreement.

articles.title_orig: Voters in Israel are deciding whether to oust Netanyahu after 3 years of war
articles.title_zh: Voters in Israel are deciding whether to oust Netanyahu after 3 years of war
articles.content_orig:
The first vote since the October 7 attacks is a tight race between Benjamin Netanyahu and ex-military chief Gadi Eisenkot — with the future direction of Israel at stake.
• Crucial election : Turnout in the first few hours of voting in Israel’s election is the highest it has been in 45 years , the country’s Central Elections Committee said. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has cast his ballot in an election seen as one of the most important in Israel’s history and a referendum on his leadership since the October 7, 2023 attacks.
• Key timings: Polls will close at 10 p.m. local time (4 p.m. ET). Opinion polls suggest the race will be too close to call, with Netanyahu in a tight race against Gadi Eisenkot , a former military chief.
• Main issues: Security and accountability are powerful electoral forces after years of war. Opinion polls suggest the economy and cost of living are also leading concerns for many voters.
• Parliamentary make-up: No single party has ever won a 61-seat majority in Israel’s 120-member parliament, or Knesset. Instead, governments are formed through alliances, which can take weeks or even months to form.
The polls in Israel’s pivotal national election – widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – are still open for about seven more hours.
Turnout in the first few hours of voting is the highest it has been in 45 years, the country’s Central Elections Committee said.
Opinion polls suggest the race will be too close to call, with Netanyahu in a tight race against centrist opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot . And many Israelis have said the choice is more consequential than ever .
Many other opposition candidates in Israel’s national elections have also already cast their votes.
In total, there are 37 parties running in the election, although most parties will fall below the threshold of votes needed to get into Israel’s parliament. Candidates can continue to campaign throughout the day, in last-minute pushes to turn out the vote.
Former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, leader of the temporarily named Bennett 2026 party, said that it’s “a fateful day for the future of our country” as he dropped his ballot in the box. Bennett voted in the city of Ra’anana, Israel.
The leader of the Democrats party, Yair Golan, cast his ballot in the city of Rosh Haayin, Israel. “A morning of great hope. In this morning, we begin the journey of rebuilding Israel (to be) better – better for its citizens, better for its prosperity and its renewed success,” Golan said as he voted
Meanwhile in Tel Aviv, opposition leader Yair Lapid voted alongside his wife.
Former Israeli Defence Minister and leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu party, Avignon Lieberman, voted in the village of Nokdim, in the occupied West Bank. Calling on everyone to “come out and vote,” Lieberman said, “I am confident that tomorrow we will wake up to a new morning, one in which we can form a Zionist coalition.”
Israelis vote for party lists, not individual candidates. In a society divided by nationality, religion, ethnicity and ideology, that produces a crowded field. There are 36 parties in play.
Dozens of lists register each cycle, but only those that pass a 3.25% vote threshold win seats and enter the 120-seat Knesset, Israel’s parliament.
Polls suggest 11 to 13 parties will meet the bar; seats are allocated through a proportional representation system.
The two largest parties are Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud and Yashar, a new centrist party led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who has emerged as his principal challenger.
What do the polls say? The latest Channel 12 opinion poll puts Eisenkot first with 23 seats, ahead of Likud with 21, though other pollsters differ. On the pro-Netanyahu Channel 14, Likud is projected to take 30 seats and Eisenkot about 20.
In head-to-head matchups about who is better suited to be prime minister, Eisenkot has led Netanyahu by a steady margin.
But coming out as the largest party is not enough to win. A prime minister needs 61 seats to form a government, and no party has ever won that majority alone. So, election night usually settles very little. The real contest is the coalition calculus that follows, which can take days, weeks or even months.
As voters across Israel head to the polls, some of the country’s leaders have already cast their ballots and are urging people to do the same.
Gadi Eisenkot, the main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in this election and head of the new Yashar party, went to the Gaza periphery to meet Gadi Mozes, one of the Israeli hostages captured during the October 7 attacks and later released by Hamas.
“I promise you that I will do everything to be worthy of your trust. That I will bring unifying leadership. That I will be prime minister of everyone – if you choose me.”
His opponents were also vocal online on Tuesday.
Defense Minister Israel Katz, a longtime Netanyahu ally, framed the election as a choice between a “decisive approach” to Israel’s security – or “a return to the policy of containment and restraint.”
President Isaac Herzog and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir both posted photos of themselves submitting their paper votes into the ballot box.
“I call on all female and male citizens of the country - we are all equal, this is our day to go, to influence and to vote,” Herzog said in a statement. “Tomorrow, we will all continue here together - we have no other country.”
Voting has begun in one of Israel’s most significant elections in its history, where voters are facing a familiar question: Should Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, stay in power?
It is the first national vote since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023 , the deadliest security failure in Israel’s history, and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran — conflicts that have mobilized much of the country and subsequently deepened Israel’s international isolation.
Here’s what’s been happening so far today:
CNN’s Tal Shalev, Oren Liebermann, Lauren Kent and Kathleen Magramo contributed to this reporting.
Opposition candidate and former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot has just voted at a polling station in the coastal city of Herzliya, in the northern part of the Tel Aviv district.
Eisenkot, the main rival to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has spent the rest of the morning visiting other polling locations to greet voters.
“I suggest not to get excited by Netanyahu’s scare tactics. … He does this in every election campaign,” Eisenkot said outside the polling station after casting his ballot.
His new party Yashar – “straight” in Hebrew – is considered centrist, and Eisenkot has primarily campaigned on issues that are domestic and address government accountability.
You can read CNN’s full profile of Eisenkot and his policies here .
In the prominent Israeli settlement of Efrat in the occupied West Bank, voters said they were focused on uniting a country that has grown more fractured and divided over the last four years.
“I hope my children will have a good place to grow up, that there will be brotherhood among us, not just wars,” Elinor Veinglas told CNN. She said she hopes “that we will remember to come together and that will be our foundation here in this country.”
Even so, Veinglas said she would only decide for whom to vote “when I see the ballots.”
Her husband, David Veinglas said he would vote for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s rival, Gadi Eisenkot. “I believe whatever comes in the end will be fine,” he told CNN. “I hope for a united government.”
Meanwhile, Haviva, who declined to give her last name, said she prays for “the people of Israel, especially that there will be unity and that they will first find what they have in common between right and left.”
Just south of Jerusalem, Efrat is more ideologically diverse community than settlements deep in the West Bank that are aligned with far-right parties. Israeli

articles.title_orig: U.K. charges 2 men arrested over alleged Iran-linked terror plot against RAF Fairford air base used by U.S.
articles.title_zh: U.K. charges 2 men arrested over alleged Iran-linked terror plot against RAF Fairford air base used by U.S.
articles.content_orig:
London — Two men have been charged with serious security offenses in Britain after being arrested in connection with the incident last month near RAF Fairford, the air base in England that had been used by the U.S. military to launch strikes on Iran, the U.K. Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Tuesday.
Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both British nationals and London residents, were charged under the 2023 National Security Act.
Abdulkarim was charged with "assisting a foreign intelligence service" in September and "engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities."
The CPS said Essghir was charged with a national security offense after he "approached or was in the vicinity of a prohibited place and his conduct was for a purpose that he knew, or having regards to other matters known to him ought reasonably to have known, was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
Both men were arrested last week on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service in a suspected plot targeting the Fairford air base in England.
Abdulkarim was arrested by Counter Terror Police under the National Security Act last week, along with another 25-year-old man — a British-Iranian dual national who was released on bail pending further investigation.
Police are still investigating a suspected terror plot against Fairford after five men were initially detained on Sept. 27 near the base in western England. All five of those men were also released on bail, but police said they remained under investigation and would be monitored.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident at the base, which prompted the U.S. Air Force to remove all of its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford . The base had been home to U.S. long-range bombers for many years, and it was used during the war with Iran to launch strikes on the Islamic Republic.
Residents of a nearby town were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police and bomb-disposal experts searched the area on Sept. 27. They found gasoline in three vans that had been driven by the five initial suspects, parked close to an entrance to the base, but no explosives.
Iranian officials have said repeatedly that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. The Iranian Embassy in London, however, said in a previous statement that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Police said Tuesday that six men remain free on bail in relation to the incident, four of whom were arrested on Sept. 27 — all U.K. nationals and London residents in their 20s — and two others who were detained subsequently, including the 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national who was detained on Oct. 1.

articles.title_orig: Climber falls nearly 5,000 feet to his death on Nepal mountain after reaching summit
articles.title_zh: Climber falls nearly 5,000 feet to his death on Nepal mountain after reaching summit
articles.content_orig:
A German climber fell about 1,500 meters (nearly 5,000 feet) to his death on Monday, a day after reaching the summit of Ama Dablam mountain, according to a trekking company operator.
Wolfgang Waschiczek, 57, was reported missing from Camp 3, which lies at around 6,200 meters. He had been resting after reaching the 6,812-meter summit on Sunday, before his planned descent.
"After a successful summit, he spent a night at Camp 3 on Sunday, and on Monday morning, his guide found him missing," Gokul Thapa, head of the trekking company Real Himalaya, told AFP.
Thapa said Waschiczek's personal trekking guide, Sonam Lama, had left him in the tent for a few minutes to return borrowed equipment, telling him to stay inside. When he returned, Waschiczek was missing.
Waschiczek's body was spotted by another Sherpa at Camp 2 at around 8 am on Monday at an altitude of about 4,600 metres, Thapa said.
The body was retrieved by helicopter during the afternoon and taken to Lukla, a town known as a gateway for mountaineers and trekkers heading to the Everest region.
It was then flown to the capital, Kathmandu, where a postmortem will be performed at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital.
"Once the postmortem is done, the body will be handed over to his family members through the embassy," Thapa told AFP.
He said this was Waschiczek's second visit to Nepal.
"He had come to Nepal in 2024 for a trek, and his passing saddened us," he added.
Two Japanese climbers died last week on another peak in west Nepal, the Reuters news agency reported .
Ama Dablam lies in Nepal's Khumbu region and is considered a technically challenging mountain with steep faces.
This is the first fatality on the mountain this year.
Last October, two climbers, one French, aged 65, and the other South Korean, aged 66, died during expeditions there.
This climbing season, more than 300 climbers are attempting to scale Ama Dablam.
Mountaineers have died on other peaks this year.
In July, famed British Nepali climber Nirmal Purja and nine other climbers were killed after being swept away by an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak.
In May, two Indian climbers died on Mount Everest during a record-breaking period of ascents via Nepal's southern route.
In May, American climber Shelley Johannesen died in an avalanche on Nepal's Mount Makalu. Johannesen, co-founder of U.S.-based outfitter Dash Adventures, had successfully reached the 27,838-foot summit before she was struck by an avalanche at around 23,600 feet while coming down.

articles.title_orig: China’s fifth plenum focuses on discipline and loyalty to Xi
articles.title_zh: China’s fifth plenum focuses on discipline and loyalty to Xi
articles.content_orig:
Plenums are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year
A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.
The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.
The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.
The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.
They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.
There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.
The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.
Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.
The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits.
Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy â branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" â to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.
According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September,  the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

articles.title_orig: GM will switch to Nasdaq from the NYSE on Nov. 17
articles.title_zh: GM will switch to Nasdaq from the NYSE on Nov. 17
articles.content_orig:
DETROIT — General Motors plans to transfer shares of its common stock from the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq as the automaker attempts to position itself more as a technology-focused company.
The Detroit automaker said Tuesday that it expects to begin trading as a Nasdaq -listed company on Nov. 17. Its ticker symbol is expected to remain "GM," the company said.
"GM's customer-focused, technology-driven strategy is creating value for our stockholders, making Nasdaq a natural home for our listing as we grow," GM CFO Paul Jacobson said in a release. "We're grateful for our long-standing partnership with the New York Stock Exchange and its remarkable legacy."
GM noted the move will provide eligibility for potential inclusion in the Nasdaq-100 Index .
Current shareholders do not need to take any action with respect to the transfer, the company said.
The switch marks a notable loss for the NYSE, as GM first listed on the exchange in 1911. The Detroit automaker also relisted on the stock exchange in 2010 following a government-backed bankruptcy.
GM follows other companies such as Walmart , DoorDash and Palantir Technologies that have transferred from the more traditional NYSE to the historically technology focused Nasdaq in recent years. Hilton Worldwide Holdings last week also announced plans to move trading from the NYSE to Nasdaq.
The key drivers for a listing transfer differ from company to company, but the Nasdaq in 2024 said common reasons include "index inclusion opportunities, cost effective fee structure, brand visibility partnership, access to Nasdaq's event space, and Nasdaq's suite of investor relations and ESG products."
GM's decision comes a week after the automaker held a technology-focused event where executives laid out the company's roadmap for artificial intelligence and self-driving vehicle technologies.
Shares of GM, which has been aggressively buying back stock , have more than doubled since 2024. GM's stock closed Monday at $76.31 per share. The company's market cap is roughly $64.4 billion.

articles.title_orig: Man charged with assisting ‘foreign intelligence service’ after incident at UK base used for Iran strikes
articles.title_zh: Man charged with assisting ‘foreign intelligence service’ after incident at UK base used for Iran strikes
articles.content_orig:
The U.K. has said it had charged a man with an offense of assisting a "foreign intelligence service" over an incident at a military base used by the U.S. for strikes on Iran.
Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, has been charged under the country's National Security Act "following an incident involving RAF Fairford," an air base in west England, prosecutors announced on Tuesday .
Between Aug. 31 and Sept. 28, Abdulkarim is alleged to have engaged in "conduct that would likely materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities", the Crown Prosecution Service added. The foreign country was not named.
Prosecutors also charged 24-year-old Nouman Essghir with "entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK".
The men are due to appear in court in London on Tuesday.
Five people were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses near RAF Fairford on Sept. 28. The base had been used as the U.S. Air Force's command outpost for operations from Europe and for American strikes on Iranian missile sites.
Announcing the charges, Frank Ferguson, a chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said that they followed "a Counter Terrorism Policing investigation into a high-profile incident involving RAF Fairford."
"We will continue to work closely with our partners as this complex investigation continues," he said.
After the arrests, U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. had moved its long-range bombers out of the U.K. in response to a threat "linked to Iran."
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers earlier this month that the incident was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard."
Over the summer, Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned it saw any military base involved in launching airstrikes on Iran as a legitimate target.
Tehran denied any involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.

articles.title_orig: Gold Steadies Above $4,000 With Fed Rate Decision in Focus
articles.title_zh: Gold Steadies Above $4,000 With Fed Rate Decision in Focus
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Gold has lost nearly a quarter of its value since the US-Iran war began. On Friday, it briefly fell to $3,975 an ounce before recovering to around $4,020 on Monday.
Yet investors have been pouring billions into gold ETFs throughout much of the decline. Gold ETF holdings have surged while prices crashed.
So, who is driving the selloff, and what happens next?
Surging oil prices have revived inflation fears, making further US interest-rate increases more likely.
The Federal Reserve raised rates in September, and markets now see roughly an 80% chance of another increase in December.
Higher rates make interest-bearing bonds more attractive than gold, which pays no yield. Last week's technology-stock selloff added pressure as investors sold assets to raise cash.
Meanwhile, CFTC data show money managers have steadily reduced bullish gold futures positions, reaching a net 104,206 contracts on October 20.
According to the World Gold Council, gold ETFs attracted a record $31 billion in the third quarter. Holdings increased by 67 tonnes in September alone, despite falling prices.
This suggests longer-term investors continued accumulating gold while speculative traders reduced exposure.
However, that support is weakening.
Global ETF holdings fell approximately 6.8 tonnes in the week of October 19, according to BoldETF, their first weekly decline since July.
The largest US gold fund, GLD, lost $2.3 billion over five days, although smaller gold ETFs attracted inflows.
The $4,000 level is now the immediate test.
Wednesday's Fed decision and Thursday's US inflation report could determine whether gold stabilizes or faces another selloff.
StoneX strategist Bob Haberkorn told Reuters he expects gold to "hang around the $4,000 level into the Fed announcement."
For investors, sustained ETF demand and easing rate expectations could support a recovery. Continued outflows and stubborn inflation would leave gold vulnerable to further losses.

articles.title_orig: Two British Men Charged Over Major Security Incident at U.K. Air Base
articles.title_zh: Two British Men Charged Over Major Security Incident at U.K. Air Base
articles.content_orig:
Oct. 27 (UPI) -- Authorities in Britain on Tuesday charged a 24-year-old man with spying for a foreign intelligence service, allegedly Iran, in relation to an incident at RAF Fairford in September in which a group of masked men in vans were arrested by counter-terrorism police near the base in the middle of the night.
The Crown Prosecution Service said in a news release that Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim of London was charged under the National Security Act with assisting a foreign intelligence service by carrying out activities in Britain between Aug. 31 and Sept. 28 "likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service."
"In this case, we believe that country to be Iran ," said Head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor.
A second man, Nouman Essghir, 24 and also from London, was charged with a single National Security offense that on Aug. 22 he entered, scoped out or got too close to a prohibited place "for a purpose prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
Both men are due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court later on Tuesday.
Five others arrested on suspicion of explosives offenses during the alleged Sept. 27 incident in the Gloucestershire village of Whelford, a half mile from the base, and then re-arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act, are free on police bail, Counter Terrorism Policing said.
CTP added that an eighth man, a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national who was re-arrested last week, has been released without charge but remains on strict police bail.
"We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state, and as the Director General of MI5 said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat," said CTP Assistant Commissioner Taylor.
RAF Fairford had been used by the U.S. military to fly missions amid its war with Iran.
A week after the security incident, the United States pulled out all of its bomber aircraft -- at least a dozen long-range B-1s -- stationed at the base, citing "threats."

articles.title_orig: Porsche profit rebounds as luxury carmaker reduces exposure to China
articles.title_zh: Porsche profit rebounds as luxury carmaker reduces exposure to China
articles.content_orig:
German sports carmaker Porsche said it has significantly reduced its exposure to China as operating profit rebounded in the first nine months of the year despite falling revenue and vehicle deliveries.
The Volkswagen-owned company published its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, announcing that operating profit was 1.74 billion euros ($1.94 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, compared with 40 million euros at the same time last year, when it booked around 2.7 billion euros in strategic restructuring costs.
Meanwhile, sales revenue fell 5.9% to 25.28 billion euros, while deliveries continued to decline, down 16% to 178,532. North America remained Porsche's largest sales region by volume.
China has historically been an important market for German luxury automakers, but they have struggled with growing competition from domestic brands, particularly in electric vehicles.
Porsche's China sales have fallen sharply in recent years amid intensifying competition from brands such as BYD, Geely and Xiaomi.
"Our geographically balanced sales footprint continues to provide resilience across different markets," Jochen Breckner, Porsche's chief financial officer, said in the earnings webcast on Tuesday.
"As you know, we have significantly reduced our exposure to China. This makes our overall business less dependent on developments from this challenging market environment."
Porsche shares were last seen trading 2.3% higher.
Porsche is also cutting thousands of jobs as part of a broader restructuring aimed at reducing costs and responding to weaker demand.
Citi analysts said in a note Tuesday that Porsche's first-nine-month results were as expected, despite challenges including China.
"Despite challenging conditions, including exceptionally low deliveries, higher costs, and higher battery electric vehicle deliveries, Porsche's underlying EBIT remains very resilient and ahead of German premium peers," the analysts said.
They added that Porsche has laid out a plan to return to double-digit underlying operating profit margins, with recovery expected to start in 2028, and net cash flow expected to rebound to above its IPO levels by 2031.
"Whilst FY27 will remain a trough year, we still see a solid, well-supported and credible multi-year EBIT and net cash recovery starting financial year 2028 - unlike many peers," the analysts said.

articles.title_orig: Israel Election Live Updates: Polls Open as Netanyahu Faces Challenge Led by Eisenkot
articles.title_zh: Israel Election Live Updates: Polls Open as Netanyahu Faces Challenge Led by Eisenkot
articles.content_orig:
Most polling shows prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition will lose its majority, with Gadi Eisenkot the leading opposition contender
What you need to know about Israel’s election
Hello and welcome to our coverage of the Israeli elections. Polls have opened in the first election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023, Israel’s subsequent destruction of Gaza, and the launch of its war with the US against Iran.
Most polling shows prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition will lose its majority in the 120-seat Knesset, but the opposition bloc will probably also fall short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.
For Netanyahu, 76, who has led the most far-right government in Israel’s history, the stakes are both political and personal. He is on trial for corruption in three separate cases, despite interventions from Donald Trump, who called for a pre-emptive pardon in the long-running saga and even wrote to Israeli president Isaac Herzog on Netanyahu’s behalf. The cases are ongoing.
It was on Netanyahu’s watch that Hamas militants broke out from Gaza three years ago to kill nearly 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians, on the deadliest day in Israel’s history. This election is widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership since those attacks.
The IDF’s globally condemned assault on Gaza , which has killed at least 75,000 people and been deemed a genocide by a UN commission , academics, legal scholars and Israeli and international rights groups, has left Israel a pariah on the world stage.
Three years of regional conflict followed the 7 October attacks, including this year’s war on Iran , which sparked an ongoing global energy crisis and has killed thousands of people, mainly in Lebanon and Iran.
What is more, under Netanyahu’s government there has been an unprecedented, aggressive surge of deadly extremist settler violence to bolster Israeli control in the occupied West Bank , as settler militants and their political backers – who have propped up Netanyahu’s government – exploited their seat at the cabinet table and expanded with impunity.
Indeed, settlement expansion has been a key feature of Netanyahu’s re-election campaign. However, it is also a driving force behind Israel’s growing international isolation, with many of its traditional allies condemning “settler terrorists” and announcing plans to impose sanctions.
Citing figures released by the Central Elections Committee, the Israeli newspaper Ynet is reporting that voter turnout in the election reached 16.68 % by 10am local time (8am GMT), the highest level recorded at that hour since 1981 .
Over 1.2m Israelis had cast their ballots by 10am, according to the data, a rise of 0.78 percentage points compared with the same stage of the previous election in 2022.
In Sanhedria cemetery in north Jerusalem , ultra-orthodox voters came to the tombs of revered rabbis before they cast their ballots. There was no question of which way they were going to vote: for the parties representing Ashkenazi and Sephardic ultra-orthodox . But some at the Sanhedria cemetery, the young especially, made clear they only would do so reluctantly.
Yair Shuker, aged 19, said only one issue was important to him. “ The election is about whether we will live by the Torah, or there will be no Torah . There will be a Jewish state or there will be no Jewish state ,” he said.
And for him - as with almost all Israel’s ultra-orthodox ( the Haredim ) - the critical measure of the state’s level of observance is whether the Haredim would continue have exemption from military service.
“There are some who study the Torah, and some who stand and defend the land,” Shuker said.
The exemption for ultra-orthodox religious students dates back to the founding the state, but has long been a sort of tension among Israeli Jews, all the more so since the 7 October attack in 2023 and the start of the Gaza war. Israel’s supreme court ruled in 2024 that the blanket exemption for haredi men had no basis in law.
In return for their support in keeping him in power, Benjamin Netanyahu promised the ultra-orthodox parties (the Sephardic party Shas and the Ashkenazi United Torah Judaism ) new legislation that would perpetuate the exemption, but has failed to deliver on that promise due to splits in his coalition. As a result both parties left the government, though Shas remained part of the coalition.
Whatever their feelings about Netanyahu, both would vote against a secular-led government led by the current opposition parties, which have pledged to end the exemption once and for all, and enforce military service if necessary.
Shuker said he did not trust either coalition, but would vote because he had been told to. “The rabbi has asked us to vote for Shas, so I will vote,” he said. A 23-year-old Ashkenazi ultra-orthodox, who identified himself as Yaacov K, expressed the same sense of disillusion mixed with duty. He said:
double quotation mark I’ll tell you the truth. To me and most of the people around me, we don’t believe in anyone .
If you’re asking me, I’ll never go and vote. But I have a rabbi and the rabbi told me listen, you have to go and vote. And if he says you have to go and vote, then that’s what I do. I don’t even start thinking if it’s worth it for me or not worth it for me.
The open distrust and contempt for Netanyahu, coupled with obedience and party discipline, could be one reason that the prime minister’s bloc has over-performed by a seat or two in past elections, compared to his poll numbers. That could be crucial if the pattern is repeated.
Azriel Zadok, a rabbi who had come for morning prayers at the Sanhedria cemetery, argued that the mass ultra-orthodox vote was essential to preserve Israel’s Jewish identity from “the left”.
“We have no problem with the secular. We pray for them, and we pray for the soldiers,” Zadok said. “ Our problem is with the leftists we are trying to decide for us how we should live .” “They want us to go to the beach on Saturday and they want us to marry outside our faith. We want to remain Jews,” the rabbi added.
The centre left is only a small part of the opposition bloc, and it does not propose to change the ultra-orthodox lifestyle. But the bloc is united on the insistence that the Haredim should do their part in the defence of the nation. It is the most divisive issue among Israeli Jews voting today .
According to Israel’s Hareetz newspaper , United Arab List ( Ra’am ), an Islamist party headed by Mansour Abbas, has filed a complaint to the Central Elections Committee, alleging that a systematic campaign has been launched to disrupt voting for the party.
In a statement, the party said police arrested several of its leading activists in southern Israel’s Negev region before dawn with no clear justification, according to Hareetz.
The party also said there is a widespread shortage of its Arabic-language ballot slips in several areas, including the cities of Nazareth and Shfaram in northern Israel. We have not yet been able to independently verify these claims.
About 15 million people live in areas under Israeli control. Just over 7 million Jewish Israelis and 1.7 million Palestinian citizens of Israel live within the country’s pre-1967 borders, known as the “green line”, and have full voting rights.
In the occupied West Bank, more than 500,000 Israeli settlers can vote. They live among 3.1 million Palestinians who are subject to military rule and do not have the right to vote .
In occupied East Jerusalem more than 230,000 Israelis with voting rights live among 350,000 Palestinians who cannot vote .
Two million Palestinians in Gaza , who live under Israeli military occupation , according to the international court of justice, also have no vote .
The Knesset, the Israeli parliament, has 120 seats, with lawmakers voted in through a system of proportional representation. No single party has ever claimed a majority of 61 seats, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions.

articles.title_orig: Big Tech just went from crushing the average stock to losing to it: Chart of the Day
articles.title_zh: Big Tech just went from crushing the average stock to losing to it: Chart of the Day
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street spent October selling chip stocks and buying toothpaste.
Consumer staples are headed for their best month in nearly five years as semiconductors crater, and the average S&P 500 stock is on track for its sharpest turnaround against the index in decades.
The AI sell-off has kept grinding through the companies leading the data center build-out , and the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) has gone nowhere with it. Its equal-weighted version ( ^SPXEW ), where the smallest company counts as much as Nvidia ( NVDA ), has pulled away.
Monday showed how fast that can flip. Chip stocks bounced, with 57 of 60 in a Yahoo Finance semiconductor basket rising, and the S&P 500 beat its equal-weighted twin.
It barely dented the month's scoreboard.
In September, the equal-weighted S&P 500 trailed the regular index by 4.5 percentage points. Through Monday, it's beating it by about 4 points in October. That swing is on track to be the largest one-month reversal in favor of the average stock since at least 1990, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
The pain is concentrated in chips. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) is down about 12% this month even after Monday's bounce. The money is going almost everywhere else, led by Energy ( XLE ), up 13%, and Staples ( XLP ), up 9%.
Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group, noted that pool, RV, and boat makers were among last week's top groups.
Investors are swapping data centers for hot tubs.
That puts equal weight on track for its first winning year against the S&P 500 since 2022.
So what's an investor to do? History offers a clue, and it hasn't been kind to years like this one.
Since 1950, midterm years have been the weakest stretch of the four-year presidential cycle, with a median S&P 500 gain of about 1%, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Detrick has pointed out that the bottom often comes right about now.
"Historically, you tend to see late October major lows in midterm years," he wrote on X , citing near-record bets on further declines. On Friday, he added that "we could be looking at another late October buying period."
Election Day is Nov. 3. The S&P 500 has been higher a year after every midterm since 1950, all 19 of them.
The payoff can take a while. In 2018, stocks kept falling after the vote, entered a bear market, and didn't bottom until Christmas Eve. And 19 elections is a small sample, especially in a year when the AI trade that powered the rally is the one cracking.
The next few weeks will tell. If stocks carve out a late-October low and the average stock keeps leading, the midterm playbook is right on schedule. If chips drag the S&P 500 to new lows after Nov. 3, 2026 is writing its own script.

articles.title_orig: China's economy is outpacing the US despite Trump's tariffs. Here's what JPMorgan says it could mean for your money
articles.title_zh: China's economy is outpacing the US despite Trump's tariffs. Here's what JPMorgan says it could mean for your money
articles.content_orig:
Voting booths are seen at Supervisor of Elections Office in Orange County, Florida, on the last business day before early voting begins for the Nov. 3, 2026, midterm elections.
William Diaz has a mantra: His only political party is his Venezuelan community.
He doesn’t abide by strict partisan rules, and doesn't believe in only voting for Democrats or Republicans. He supported Republicans Sen. Rick Scott and Secretary of State Marco Rubio when they were running for office in Florida , where Diaz has lived for 37 years.
For these midterm elections, however, the Orlando resident hopes to make a clear statement: He does not support President Donald Trump’s immigration policies and is unhappy with how Republican-backed initiatives have affected his community.
Read More: An Idaho ICE Raid Rounded Up Hundreds. The Fallout Could Change How ICE Operates
“I voted already, and what I did when I was voting and when I was with my ballot, I was really thinking and praying for all those that has no voice, those that can not vote, those immigrants that are right now victim of actions on the streets,” Diaz tells TIME, referring to Trump’s mass deportation agenda and the expansive influence of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). “My people have been suffering that much.”
Diaz is one of more than 2.6 million people who have already cast ballots in Florida, either by mail or through in-person early voting, according to state figures released Sunday. In-person early voting began in some counties Oct. 19 and expanded statewide Oct. 24.
Diaz’s community is one part of a Florida Latino electorate with varied national origins and political loyalties. Taken together, however, Latino voters are a swing vote in several closely watched races statewide. They were key to Trump’s Florida victory in 2024, with 56% supporting him over Kamala Harris, according to the 2024 American Electorate Voter Poll .
But new polls ahead of Election Day suggest that Latino support for the GOP may be on shaky ground—a shift that could put Republicans to the test in Florida and shape the political landscape beyond November.
Dissatisfaction among Florida’s Latino voters reflects a broader national mood, according to Stephanie Valencia, a co-founder of Equis Research, an organization that studies Latino voting behavior.
Concerns about the economy and immigration enforcement tactics are fueling dissatisfaction among Latino voters, who “make up a huge part of the electorate in Florida,” she says, pointing out that both of these issues are “disproportionately impacting” them.
A Univision/YouGov poll, conducted Oct. 2–15, showed that 41% of registered Latino voters in Florida were “very or somewhat worried” that they, a family member, or someone close could be detained or otherwise directly affected by immigration enforcement, compared with 27% of Florida voters overall.
The same poll showed that 4 in 10 Latino voters in the state felt that their finances had worsened over the past year, with 70% disapproving of Trump’s handling of the cost of living in the U.S. That stands in comparison to a 63% disapproval rate from Florida voters overall.
Read More: Midterm Ad Spending Has Surpassed $10B. Where Is the Money Coming From?
For Johanna Chavez, a Dominican immigrant living in Kissimmee, Florida, the economy is top of mind.
“Many people are concerned about the economy and the price of gasoline … and then there’s the cost of rent, it’s become incredibly, overwhelmingly high,” Chavez, who speaks Spanish, tells TIME through a translator. “All the things they promised would be done—nothing has happened.”
In the past few years, Chavez says it has felt like the United States has started “regressing,” and the opportunities she was looking for when she arrived here have not materialized in the way she had hoped.
“It’s starting to feel just like the situation back in my home country, the Dominican Republic,” she says. “We all came here hoping for change, seeking a better life, but it’s ending up being the same thing all over again. Things just aren’t what they’re supposed to be.”
Jared Nordlund, the Florida State Advocacy Director at UnidosUS, the largest nonprofit Latino rights organization in the U.S., says this is a common refrain among Floridian Latinos; people are upset over how the economy has been affected by tariffs and the war in Iran . Florida was hit particularly hard by rising gas prices after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz squeezed the global energy supply, he says.
“Florida is not a state friendly for public transportation, so people are highly reliant on the cars, and so what they would be paying for food now is having to kind of get broke between … paying to get the gas and then going to get food,” Nordlund says.
The question now is whether that dissatisfaction will translate into votes against Republicans—and whether it will be enough to tip the state’s close races.
Trump’s approval rating has plummeted with Latino voters in Florida, dropping from 58% approval at the start of his term to 36% ahead of midterm elections, according to Equis Research.
According to an AP-NORC poll from October, about 6 in 10 Latino voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the presidency, and more than 7 in 10 disapprove of how he is handling the economy.
A Pew Research Center poll found that Trump’s job approval rating among Latino voters dropped from 38% in February 2025 to 24% in September and October. Of those who backed him in the last election, approval dropped to 57%—down from 93% in early 2025.
The shift may be resonating with Republicans like Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, who is seeking re-election in Florida’s 27th District in Miami-Dade—a majority Latino district that Trump carried by some 15 points in 2024. She publicly broke with Trump in her campaign and criticized his immigration policies.
In one ad in September, Salazar said that Trump has “gone too far" with his deportation agenda.
“In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record,” she notes in the ad.
“Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” Salazar continues, addressing Trump. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”
Guillermo Grenier, a Cuban American professor of sociology at Florida International University (FIU), agrees that many Latino voters are “ticked off” at Trump.
“The population, if you look at the whole Latino conglomerate, is turned off pretty strongly with Trump,” he says.
But South Florida’s Latino electorate is unique; Grenier points out that the state is home to 1.9 million Cuban Americans—the largest concentration in the United States.
As a voting bloc, the community has significant sway. In 2024, FIU’s Cuba poll found that 68% of likely Cuban American voters in Miami-Dade County supported Trump, compared to 23% for Harris—representing his highest-recorded support level in the poll's history.
A shift away from Republicans among Cuban American voters could therefore have significant consequences in South Florida. But disillusionment doesn’t always turn into action, according to Grenier.
“I think a lot of Cubans are pissed off at Trump, but they're still Republicans,” he says.
The Democratic Party’s response to this potential opening may unfold over several election cycles.
“Democrats are going to be in a probationary period with Latinos and with all voters, quite frankly, on whether they can deliver or not,” Valencia says. “One election is not durable support among a particular group.”
The electorate’s age also matters to its long-term political influence, says Michael McDonald, a professor of political science at the University of Florida. “Latinos are much younger than the rest of the population in the United States.”
He points out that voter turnout “is highly correlated with age” and expects Latino participation to increase as younger voters grow older. In his assessment, that could reshape the electoral map beyond
