articles.title_orig: From the Mediterranean to the dinner table
articles.title_zh: From the Mediterranean to the dinner table
articles.content_orig:
Bluefin tuna does not forgive delay. The fatty belly — otoro — is prized for a richness that seems to dissolve on the tongue, a quality built on gloss, deep color and a marine intensity that no cooked fish can replicate. That pleasure lasts only as long as the cold chain holds. A few hours of warmth, a break in handling, and the texture turns from silk to something far less forgiving.
Delivering bluefin at its best is therefore an industrial problem disguised as a culinary one. The fish must move from sea to ultra-low-temperature storage quickly, in volume, and without interruption.
The Ocean Star exists for that problem. It is a floating cold-chain hub that links Maltese harvesting expertise with Chinese cold-chain capacity.
It is an ultra-low-temperature processing and transportation vessel owned by Mediterranean Bluefin Industry Development (Hainan), a China-Malta joint venture specializing in bluefin tuna processing and trade.
The joint venture was established in June 2024 by Malta Fish Farming Ltd, or MFF, and China's Shandong Far-sea Development Ltd, covering trade, transportation and processing.
The vessel began a new production season in late September, operating in the Mediterranean east of Malta.
Workers weigh tuna on its decks, move product into refrigerated rooms, and dock at Valletta Port — images that trace the journey from harvest to cold storage.
MFF Chairman Salvu Ellul described the Ocean Star as the first ultra-low-temperature refrigerated transport and processing vessel and said it had become the most efficient bluefin tuna processing platform in the Mediterranean region.
He made the remarks on Oct 11 while briefing China's Ambassador to Malta, Zhang Zuo, during a visit to the Valletta waterfront in October.
Ellul told the ambassador that cooperation between the two nations in the fisheries sector had expanded year by year and that there were high expectations the partnership would serve as a bridge for economic and trade exchanges between China and Malta.
Ellul pointed to the Belt and Road Initiative as a source of trade opportunities, saying that Malta Fish Farming would ride the wind and waves to bring Malta's highest quality bluefin tuna products to the consumers' table worldwide.

articles.title_orig: Dollar General overcharged millions at checkout for years, FTC and 20 states allege
articles.title_zh: Dollar General overcharged millions at checkout for years, FTC and 20 states allege
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states on Monday sued Dollar General, accusing the budget retailer of charging customers more for products than it advertised.
The chain, which operates 21,000 stores nationwide, allegedly mislabeled prices for years, "extracting millions of dollars in unlawful overcharges," the FTC alleged.
"Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last," Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement .
The FTC added that American consumers depend on Dollar General's advertised low prices to make ends meet on tight budgets, while prices that don't reflect advertised deals make it impossible for them to manage household finances.
The agency filed its complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, Dollar General's home state.
"Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store," Dollar General said in a statement. "As with other retailers and despite our policies and procedures, occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement."
Dollar General said it was made aware of the FTC's investigation in early February.
According to the suit, thousands of Dollar General stores unlawfully overcharged shoppers.
Dollar General "has for years engaged in deceptive conduct that harms the very consumers it claims to serve," the FTC and states allege in the suit. "Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags, and advertisements. This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country."
The company also faced thousands of consumer complaints claiming it failed to honor advertised prices at checkout, a sign Dollar General knowingly harmed customers, according to the FTC.
The suit seeks a permanent injunction, along with monetary and other relief.
Dollar General in its statement said, "FTC staff also demanded a monetary amount that was untethered to — and orders of magnitude larger than — any realistic assessment of amounts attributable to pricing discrepancies."
The company said it "worked tirelessly and in good faith to resolve this matter without litigation," including an "alternative, and in our view, more reasonable, manner of calculating potential settlement ranges."
"Although we respect the FTC's role in protecting American consumers and the State representatives' role in protecting the citizens of their respective states, we will defend this litigation vigorously," it said.

articles.title_orig: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
articles.title_zh: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
articles.content_orig:
China and Russia are tightening their grip on Arctic shipping routes, turning the rapidly warming region into a new geopolitical battleground with Europe.
Moscow and Beijing last week have agreed to expand freight traffic along Arctic shipping corridors , increase services between their ports and deepen cooperation on building polar vessels.
The agreement came after the EU unveiled a new Arctic strategy aimed at countering growing Russian and Chinese influence in the region.
Although the competing moves underscore how the once-remote region is turning into a strategic prize, analysts said that Europe's ability to challenge the emerging China-Russia partnership remains limited, given Moscow's control over the main shipping corridor and Beijing's growing commercial clout.
That's because Moscow controls the Northern Sea Route, including shipping permits, transit fees and a vast fleet of nuclear icebreakers, while Beijing provides the cargo, vessels and industrial capacity needed to develop the corridor, she added.
Europe, by contrast, has limited icebreaker capacity and Arctic infrastructure, leaving it with little leverage to challenge the partnership despite its position as a major destination market.
The Northern Sea Route offers itself as an increasingly attractive alternative, as Middle East disruptions expose vulnerabilities in established shipping corridors.
Cargo traveling between Asia and Europe through the Northern Sea Route could have its journey shortened to between 18 to 22 days, down approximately 35% from the 28 to 35 day journey through Suez, according to data provided by Fertmax FZCO.
For Moscow, the route offers an opportunity to redirect energy exports toward Asia as Western sanctions constrain its access to European markets, said industry watchers whom CNBC spoke to.
On the other hand, it provides Beijing another trade artery that could reduce reliance on traditional maritime chokepoints.
David Roche, a veteran strategist at Quantum Strategy & Geonomics, said the Arctic's importance lies less in its potential to transform global shipping than in the deepening economic dependence between Russia and China.
"The significance of the arctic route is for Russian energy shipments to China, which will increase China's control over Russia in terms of Russia's dependence on China to sell its energy to compensate for losses of its gas markets in Europe," Roche highlighted.
The EU has acknowledged the growing challenge, highlighting the region's strategic value in its strategy, as mentioned by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas last week .
Europe isn't entirely without leverage.
The EU's new strategy calls for expanding European icebreaker capacity, strengthening maritime surveillance and developing infrastructure linking Arctic trade networks to European markets.
It also proposes a maritime security hub and greater protection for undersea cables, reflecting growing concerns about Russian military activity and threats to critical infrastructure.
Yet those strengths may not be enough to overturn the structural advantages enjoyed by Moscow and Beijing, said experts.
Garcia-Herrero said Europe's leverage largely rests on its position as a major destination market and the presence of large shipping companies that have avoided the Arctic because of environmental and commercial risks.
Europe also faces a strategic dilemma: engaging with the emerging corridor could deepen its reliance on Russian-controlled infrastructure, even as it seeks to reduce Moscow's economic influence.
Fertmax FZCO's former global head of research, Daeijin Lee said Western operators face sanctions, insurance and compliance complications that make the route considerably less attractive than it is for Chinese companies.
"The Arctic gives diversification, not independence," he said.
For all the geopolitical attention, the Arctic remains a marginal player in global shipping.
Roche estimates Arctic trade accounts for roughly 0.3% of global shipping today and could reach about 1% by 2030.
Data from Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom and CNBC calculations based on UN Trade and Development figures similarly supports the 0.3% figure, with 37.02 million tonnes of cargo transiting the Northern Sea Route in 2025 compared to the 12.72 billion tonnes of global seaborne trade in 2024.
Only 3.2 million tonnes of that cargo, or less than a tenth, involved vessels transiting the entire route, rather than shipments originating or terminating in the Russian Arctic, according to the Centre for High North Logistics .
But traffic may be picking up, the latest September 2026 CHNL data showed.
The route recorded 104 confirmed transit voyages carrying an estimated 3.7 million tonnes of cargo by the end of September, exceeding the 3.2 million tonnes recorded during the entire 2025 navigation season.
Much of the existing traffic consists of Russian oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities rather than international container shipments.
However, the route also faces significant commercial hurdles. Ice conditions restrict navigation for much of the year, while specialized vessels, insurance premiums and Russian transit fees can erode savings from shorter voyages.
Matthew Wright, an analyst at Kpler, said the route remains poorly suited to replacing established shipping corridors because operators need reliable, year-round services.
Lee similarly expects the Arctic to develop primarily as a seasonal express route for selected high-value cargo rather than a replacement for Suez.
However, climate change could shift the balance in the long-term.
A study published in the WMU Journal of Maritime Affairs projected that melting Polar ice could increase the Northern Sea Route's annual transit capacity to between 127 million and 463 million tonnes by 2050.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu's political survival on the line as Israel votes
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu's political survival on the line as Israel votes
articles.content_orig:
An extremely tight race into Israel's election Tuesday, has some citizens flying back into the country to cast their votes.
Israel doesn't allow votes from abroad, except from those serving in the country's diplomatic missions. As many as 80,000 Israelis living outside the country are expected to come back to vote in Tuesday's election, according to estimates from one group helping to organize citizens living outside the country. Israel has about 7.3 million eligible voters , according to the Washington-based International Foundation for Electoral Systems.
"While not a large block, the 80,000 that may return home to participate could make a big difference in the final count of a very tight election," said Yael Shomer, a professor of political science at Tel Aviv University.
In Israel's first election since 2022, Benjamin Netanyahu of the Likud party, who has served as Prime Minister for 18 years over three separate periods, is facing top challenger Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, who heads the Yashar party. Both would likely need backing from potential coalition partners in order to win.
Polls are extremely tight heading into Tuesday's election. Issues like security, already a major decider for Israelis, have gotten even more contentious with the Iran war in full swing. The exemption of some ultra-Orthodox men from conscription is also causing a great divide in Israeli society, while Prime Minister Netanyahu is still working on a controversial plan that would give the governing coalition more control over the judiciary.
"All elections in Israel are energetic, but because this one will have such a meaningful impact on the future of the country it has been especially hard fought," Shomer said. "This election is really about how we see our future, voter turnout will be very high."
Voter turnout in 2022 was just above 70% according to Israel's Central Elections Committee. Pollsters believe it could reach as high as 87% this time. Among foreign service workers serving in embassies and consulates outside of Israel, voter turnout was 90%. According to The Central Elections Committee, that number is usually closer to 70%.
In order to help those living abroad come back to cast votes, an organization called Fly & Vote was set up by the America-Israel Democracy Coalition , a U.S.-based group which was originally created in 2023 to stop the effort by Likud to reform the judicial system.
While organizations and political parties are prohibited from paying for any kind of transportation for people inside or outside of Israel, Aid Coalition has found other ways to facilitate the voting.
Fly & Vote, which has been funded by private donations, chartered a flight for Israelis living in Portugal and bought blocks of tickets for flights from the New York area. Anyone on the flights had to pay for their own seats.
"Israelis who don't live here still have a stake in what we do, and we want to help them," said Ora Peled-Nakash, the group's co-founder. "We don't take a political position though and we don't tell anyone how to vote, we just help them cast their ballot."
Travelers will also have plenty of commercial options.
For decades El Al was the only Israeli airline to fly routes from the U.S. to Israel. Arkia started offering flights last year and Israir earlier this year. Legacy U.S. carriers United and Delta are also flying to Israel again after suspending flights due to the war with Iran. Germany's Lufthansa flies to Israel from Europe and British Airways is scheduled to re-start flights this week.
What's more, the price is in line with what it would be during normal times, Peled-Nakash said. There were still a few seats left on El Al flights from JFK or Newark airports ranging from $1,300 to $2,500 as of Sunday, according to research from CNBC.
After years of political instability that saw five elections between 2019 and 2022, Tueday's election result could help shape Israel's political, security and economic direction for years to come. But it also shows how politically divided the country has become.

articles.title_orig: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders
articles.title_zh: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders
articles.content_orig:
The fifth plenum comes against a backdrop of years of purges that have had some analysts wondering if the issue is corruption or a lack of loyalty
When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level.
As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials kick off an important meeting this week, discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions.
The “fifth plenum” began on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption .
As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge.
Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said.
He added that in the CCP system, “corruption is not just material things”, but also “spiritual corruption”, which includes political disloyalty.
Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.
Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: “Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party’s.
“Xi’s answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done,” Thomas said.
The job may be never ending, but the plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party’s energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP’s Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy.
The meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year’s 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.
Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party’s credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. “It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi’s] worldview,” said Brown. “Everyone else is corrupt”.
In the past, Xi has warned that the party could “lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history” if it could not get its house in order. “This is by no means an exaggeration,” he said.
The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders.
In January, Zhang Youxia , China’s top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military’s top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC)
A host of other purges means that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC’s head of discipline.
Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing.
Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi’s political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.
Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are “the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline”.

articles.title_orig: Jordan says it attacked militants in Syria tied to church assault. Syria says civilians killed
articles.title_zh: Jordan says it attacked militants in Syria tied to church assault. Syria says civilians killed
articles.content_orig:
Jordanian air force says it carried out strikes against ‘terrorist groups’ tied to killing of nine in Karak
Jordan has carried out airstrikes against armed groups in Syria in retaliation for Friday’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the southern Jordanian city of Karak that killed nine people, the Jordanian air force has said in a statement.
It said the operation “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”. It did not specify who the groups were or the precise location of the strikes.
Syrian state media reported that civilians had been killed in the strikes. The director of health in the southern province of Daraa, where the strikes took place, told the Syrian national news agency, Sana, that at least five civilians had been killed, including women and children and a 65-year-old man.
Jordan’s armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus, but Syria’s government gave a contradictory account, saying it had launched an investigation into the ⁠Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security coordination in border areas.
In the aftermath of the strikes, Syria said it had closed the ⁠Nassib border crossing with Jordan, suspending ⁠traffic in both directions. Nassib is Jordan’s only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria.
Earlier on Monday, Jordanian authorities arrested three men for last week’s attack, which also wounded more than two dozen people. The arrests followed a dawn shootout, and all three men were wounded, officials said.
The attack struck the Greek Orthodox church during a funeral in Karak, about 55 miles (90km) south of the capital, Amman, on Friday. Karak is home to a minority Christian population.
The attack shocked the nation, and Jordan declared three days of mourning for the victims. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack; the attackers’ motive remained unknown.
Later on Monday, Jordan’s Public Security Directorate identified the three arrested men as brothers Hazzah Zaidan Mohammad and Mishal Zaidan Mohammad, and their brother-in-law Ahmad Sami Hussein. All three are Jordanian; they were taken into custody in Karak, south of Amman.
The agency’s chief described the gunmen as “takfiri”, a term used for Sunni militants, but said they were not tied to any organised group.
“They only represent themselves,” Maj Gen Obaidallah Abd Rabbo Al-Maayta told a news conference. He also said a large cache of munitions was found in the abandoned house where Jordanian forces apprehended the men.
Jordan’s interior minister, Mazen al-Faraya, said the attack by the three men was the result of “a terroristic, extremist way of thinking”.
“If this way of thinking is not resolved, we will see incidents like this again,” he told reporters.
Jordan’s King Abdullah II had ordered authorities to respond with “an iron fist” against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.
“We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he said in a statement on Monday.
Relatives of the victims said the arrests brought them some relief.
“Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief, and the grief of the Jordanian people – not just for us, the families of the martyrs,” Khaled al-Borqan, himself a survivor of the attack and a relative of three of the people killed, told Al-Mamlaka.
“Despite the sadness and pain, the news brought us joy,” Fares Halaseh, an uncle of one of the victims and a survivor of the attack, told the TV station.
But the pain remains, he added. “We will not forget this agony for years to come.”

articles.title_orig: Israeli election draws tens of thousands of citizens flying back to vote
articles.title_zh: Israeli election draws tens of thousands of citizens flying back to vote
articles.content_orig:
An extremely tight race into Israel's election Tuesday, has some citizens flying back into the country to cast their votes.
Israel doesn't allow votes from abroad, except from those serving in the country's diplomatic missions. As many as 80,000 Israelis living outside the country are expected to come back to vote in Tuesday's election, according to estimates from one group helping to organize citizens living outside the country. Israel has about 7.3 million eligible voters , according to the Washington-based International Foundation for Electoral Systems.
"While not a large block, the 80,000 that may return home to participate could make a big difference in the final count of a very tight election," said Yael Shomer, a professor of political science at Tel Aviv University.
In Israel's first election since 2022, Benjamin Netanyahu of the Likud party, who has served as Prime Minister for 18 years over three separate periods, is facing top challenger Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, who heads the Yashar party. Both would likely need backing from potential coalition partners in order to win.
Polls are extremely tight heading into Tuesday's election. Issues like security, already a major decider for Israelis, have gotten even more contentious with the Iran war in full swing. The exemption of some ultra-Orthodox men from conscription is also causing a great divide in Israeli society, while Prime Minister Netanyahu is still working on a controversial plan that would give the governing coalition more control over the judiciary.
"All elections in Israel are energetic, but because this one will have such a meaningful impact on the future of the country it has been especially hard fought," Shomer said. "This election is really about how we see our future, voter turnout will be very high."
Voter turnout in 2022 was just above 70% according to Israel's Central Elections Committee. Pollsters believe it could reach as high as 87% this time. Among foreign service workers serving in embassies and consulates outside of Israel, voter turnout was 90%. According to The Central Elections Committee, that number is usually closer to 70%.
In order to help those living abroad come back to cast votes, an organization called Fly & Vote was set up by the America-Israel Democracy Coalition , a U.S.-based group which was originally created in 2023 to stop the effort by Likud to reform the judicial system.
While organizations and political parties are prohibited from paying for any kind of transportation for people inside or outside of Israel, Aid Coalition has found other ways to facilitate the voting.
Fly & Vote, which has been funded by private donations, chartered a flight for Israelis living in Portugal and bought blocks of tickets for flights from the New York area. Anyone on the flights had to pay for their own seats.
"Israelis who don't live here still have a stake in what we do, and we want to help them," said Ora Peled-Nakash, the group's co-founder. "We don't take a political position though and we don't tell anyone how to vote, we just help them cast their ballot."
Travelers will also have plenty of commercial options.
For decades El Al was the only Israeli airline to fly routes from the U.S. to Israel. Arkia started offering flights last year and Israir earlier this year. Legacy U.S. carriers United and Delta are also flying to Israel again after suspending flights due to the war with Iran. Germany's Lufthansa flies to Israel from Europe and British Airways is scheduled to re-start flights this week.
What's more, the price is in line with what it would be during normal times, Peled-Nakash said. There were still a few seats left on El Al flights from JFK or Newark airports ranging from $1,300 to $2,500 as of Sunday, according to research from CNBC.
After years of political instability that saw five elections between 2019 and 2022, Tueday's election result could help shape Israel's political, security and economic direction for years to come. But it also shows how politically divided the country has become.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI says its AI model has disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis
articles.title_zh: OpenAI says its AI model has disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of computer science papers rest on a conjecture that an internal OpenAI model now claims to have refuted, the company said on Monday. OpenAI announced two more results the same day, one in mathematics and one in physics.
In a blog post , OpenAI said the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) has been “widely believed to be true”. The conjecture concerns how hard it is to solve Boolean satisfiability, a problem closely tied to P versus NP. Researchers have used it to show that problems in graph theory, computational biology, databases and other fields are hard to solve quickly.
According to OpenAI, its model found the disproof on 16 October. The company checked it in Lean, a language that verifies proofs by machine, the next day. It has published the model’s write-up and the Lean proof on GitHub.
A group led by Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi of UC San Diego and Ryan Williams of MIT will check and explain the result. Impagliazzo and Paturi first proposed ETH with Francis Zane.
An internal model at OpenAI has produced a claimed refutation of ETH! Russell Impagliazzo, Mohan Paturi, and I have been asked to help organize an open and independent examination of this claim. 1/4
Ryan Williams @rrwilliams.bsky.social (@rrwilliams) October 26, 2026
In an open letter to their field, the three researchers said their role is not an endorsement.
“Our involvement should not be taken as certification of the claim. A result of this significance requires careful, independent scrutiny,” Impagliazzo, Paturi and Williams wrote.
Williams said on X that the group signed no non-disclosure agreements and will not be paid. The group asked OpenAI to release all its raw data on the ETH result and to fund a conference for the research community. OpenAI agreed to both, according to Williams and OpenAI.
In mathematics, OpenAI says its models proved the local smoothing conjecture, which Christopher Sogge proposed in 1991, in every dimension. That would also settle the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions. Mathematicians had proved local smoothing in two dimensions in 2019 and the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions in 2025. OpenAI released the model’s write-up and a Lean proof, as it did with the 722 maths papers it published on 6 October.
In physics, OpenAI says its models produced a rigorous proof that certain quantum field theories exist in four dimensions. These include quantum chromodynamics, which describes the strong force between quarks and gluons. The work includes a proof that pure Yang-Mills theory exists, which is part of one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s Millennium Prize problems. OpenAI said in September it would not claim the prize for its Navier-Stokes proof .
Nobel laureate David Gross will lead the physics group, with Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov and Nikita Nekrasov. That group chose not to release the AI-produced material for now and will write up the work itself.
OpenAI says it does not seek academic credit for the discoveries. It says the researchers in each group should get the recognition for the explanations they write. It has also given $5m to the Simons Foundation for workshops and conferences on AI-produced results.
The three computer scientists ask in their letter how credit should work when AI finds results first. They warn that recognition may go to those who publish first or have the most powerful tools, while checking and explaining the work gets less credit. Mathematicians raised similar concerns in the Leiden declaration in June.
“If the claim is correct, it will change an important part of theoretical computer science,” the three researchers wrote.

articles.content_orig:
A United States appeals court has ruled against the administration of President Donald Trump in its bid to block the state of California from counting certain mail-in ballots this election cycle.
In a decision on Monday, the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals denied a request from the government to sequester roughly 20,000 mailed ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm election.
The Trump administration had asserted that the ballots were sent to people who are “likely” non-citizens.
But it has not publicly revealed how it created its list or determined that the voters identified upon it were ineligible due to their citizenship status.
In a two-to-one decision, the appeals court said the Trump administration had not given lower courts enough time to review the case. It therefore declined to stop California’s ballot tabulation.
The court’s majority also underscored that election administration was the state’s responsibility under the US Constitution.
The Trump administration was asking “the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain”, Judge Gabriel Sanchez wrote in his opinion.
Sanchez also warned that granting the Trump administration’s petition would be “inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike”.
The Trump administration filed its lawsuit against California on October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm vote on November 3.
California is a Democrat-led state, and Trump, a Republican leader, has repeatedly made unfounded claims that the state is prone to “cheating” in its elections.
The case is currently being weighed in a lower court, with a hearing scheduled for Tuesday.
But the Trump administration sought an expedited decision from the appeals court, pointing to the looming election date.
The midterm elections are critical to determine which political party holds power in Congress.
Currently, the Republican Party maintains slim majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, but experts project the Democratic Party is on track to make significant gains, flipping one or both chambers.
In the lead-up to the midterms, Trump has raised the prospect of non-citizen voting as a threat to election integrity.
But experts say such voting is rare. California officials have likewise cast doubt on the administration’s claims of 20,000 ballots going to “likely non-citizens”, and they framed the administration’s lawsuit as an effort to interfere in the voting process.
“At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a court filing on October 20. “At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”
Trump’s Department of Justice has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for complete access to voter rolls that include sensitive personal data.
It has argued that releasing such information is necessary to prevent alleged voter fraud.
But the department has lost 26 of those cases thus far, with opponents successfully arguing that such manoeuvres could scare away voters and interfere with state election administration.
The Trump administration has yet to win any of the 30 cases.
Despite claims to the contrary by Trump and his allies, cases of illegal voting, including by non-citizens, are few and far between. Non-citizens are barred from participating in federal elections in all 50 states in the US.
In July, an investigation by the news service Reuters found only 129 cases of noncitizens being charged by federal authorities with illegal voting since 1996.
Many of those cases involved mistakes, like administrative errors or individuals being uncertain of voting rules, rather than fraudulent intent.
Voting rights advocates have also pointed to flaws in how the Trump administration has identified potential non-citizen voting, signalling some eligible voters may be disenfranchised as part of its efforts.
Immigration agents under Trump have been assigned to ferret out non-citizen voters, in some cases knocking on doors to inquire about the citizenship status of the residents inside.
Last week, the administration charged 28 immigrants in California with illegally voting.
But reporting from the Los Angeles Times found that some of the accused reacted to the charges with confusion and maintained that they never registered to vote.
Trump has a history of promoting false claims of election fraud in order to justify greater federal influence over the voting process.
In 2020, he lost his bid for re-election to Democrat Joe Biden, but he denied his defeat, instead blaming vote “rigging”. That claim prompted some of Trump’s supporters to storm the US Capitol on January 6, 2023, in an apparent effort to halt the election certification.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market News, Oct. 26, 2026: Tech Shares Rally After Anthropic Files for Historic IPO
articles.title_zh: Stock Market News, Oct. 26, 2026: Tech Shares Rally After Anthropic Files for Historic IPO
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
ORLANDO, Florida, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Stocks mostly rose on Monday, lifted by renewed optimism around AI as Anthropic filed for a US IPO and as investors awaited more 'Big Tech' earnings later this week. Weaker oil prices also support risk appetite.
The big exception, however, was Brazil, where financial assets plunged ‌following left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's shock win in Sunday's presidential election.
In my column today, I look at whether 'stagflation' pressures may be building in the US. ‌A deflating artificial intelligence bubble puts downward pressure on Wall Street and wider economic growth, but the revival of oil and energy prices is putting upward pressure on inflation. It's a tricky one for investors, and the ​Fed.
• Brazil stocks, real tumble as Lula win ends bullish run
• Anthropic's IPO filing shows explosive growth, risks and staggering costs
• Meta eyes record $95 billion equity raise to fund AI expansion
• In China, the AI bubble has already burst
• Fed to hit pause on rate hikes, but maybe not for long
• Today's Key Market Moves STOCKS: Brazil -14%. Asia mixed, Europe and UK up around 0.8%. Wall Street higher: Nasdaq +0.8%, S&P 500 +0.7%, Dow +0.3%.SECTORS/SHARES: Seven sectors on the S&P 500 rise, four fall. Tech +1.5%, comms services -1.4%. Tesla +5%, DoorDash -6%.FX: Brazilian real -8.5%, biggest fall since devaluation in 1999. Philippine peso sinks ‌to record low near 64.00/$. US dollar index edges higher.BONDS: ⁠Brazil buys back bonds, cancels auctions. US 2-year auction is ok — foreign demand dips, domestic demand surges.COMMODITIES/METALS: Oil slips — Brent -0.8%, WTI -1.5%. Gold +0.5% back above $4,000/oz.
If investors were showing signs of AI fatigue in recent weeks, they're hiding it well as this week gets underway. On Monday, ⁠Anthropic filed for a US IPO, Meta announced plans for a $95 billion equity raise, and SpaceX said it has struck a $40 billion deal with Apollo Global Management for AI chip funding. The Anthropic IPO could value the company at a record-breaking $1.5 trillion or more, and Meta's capital raise would also be a record.
The eye-popping sums needed to fund the AI buildout have begun to suck some of the ​air ​out of the AI bubble, but that was shrugged off on Monday, at least temporarily — tech and AI ​stocks fueled a solid rebound on Wall Street. Competition for investor ‌capital is heating up.
Politically, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's surprise election victory on Sunday was truly historic: never before had a candidate won the decisive second-round vote after losing the first. It also means a record-setting fourth term for Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday. Unsurprisingly, given the historic significance of Lula's comeback, there was a reaction across Brazilian markets.
Few doubt the scale of Brazil's fiscal and economic challenges, but Monday's collapse in Brazilian assets is likely to reverse, to some degree. Part of the selloff was because investors were caught so flat-footed. As late as Sunday, prediction markets were pointing to an 80% chance of a win for Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. But Lula's scope to push through an agenda that investors fear will ‌be limited, due to Bolsonaro's backing in Congress.
This week is one of the busiest in years ​for policymaking in the world's developed economies, with half of the G10 central banks set to decide interest ​rates. Monetary authorities in New Zealand and Canada are widely expected to hike by ​25 basis points, while those in the US, euro zone and Japan are expected to keep them on hold but signal possible increases in ‌December.
The common enemy is inflation, which is already too sticky in many ​countries. Oil and global energy prices remain elevated ​as war continues to choke Middle East supply routes, and the worry for policymakers is this bleeds into core inflation and becomes embedded in inflation expectations. But if the AI bubble deflates, growth, consumer confidence and investor sentiment could deflate too, putting policymakers in an even tighter bind.
What could move markets tomorrow?
• Japan services producer price inflation (September)
• ​South Korea GDP (Q3, advance)
• US Treasury sells $70 billion of 5-year notes ‌at auction
• US durable goods (September)
• Corporate earnings, including Visa, Coca-Cola, Boeing, Seagate Technology, HSBC, Novartis

Joseph Servi joined Goldman Sachs this month as a managing director in New York for AI infrastructure investment banking with a focus on data centres, GPUs and fiber optics. He spent the last two years at SMBC as co-head of its asset-backed securities (ABS) division as well as head of digital infrastructure and esoteric ABS origination. The role involved packaging the assets of AI infrastructure firms into securitized bonds or other products that are sold to investors. It's not clear exactly what his new role at Goldman will entail; the bank declined to comment.
Servi also previously worked in private equity as a principal with KKR working on structured capital markets for its digital infrastructure team.
Data centre ABS is a booming field; Barclays Research reported in July that outstanding issuance had grown to $61bn in 2026, up from $4bn in 2020. Some AI firms are instead using their assets as collateral for loans. CoreWeave raised $8.5bn earlier this year backed by its chips and a contract with Meta. As scrutiny of these firms increases, the need to package their financing arrangements well may become more important.

articles.title_orig: DOJ charges ex-FBI Director James Comey in new case
articles.title_zh: DOJ charges ex-FBI Director James Comey in new case
articles.content_orig:
Former FBI Director James Comey has been charged for the third time with federal crimes, according to a court filing made public Monday.
Comey is charged in the new case with knowingly communicating information related to national defense to a person not entitled to receive it. He is also charged with conspiring with others to violate the law against sharing such information.
The criminal complaint in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C. says Comey, "through one or more co-conspirators," directed an unnamed individual "to disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication."
Comey has been repeatedly targeted by the Department of Justice under the administration of President Donald Trump , who fired him as FBI director in 2017. Both men have been fierce critics of one another since then.
Comey is currently seeking the dismissal of an indictment obtained by the DOJ in North Carolina federal court on charges of threatening Trump's life by posting a photo of seashells on a beach on social media. He previously successfully won dismissal of another indictment accusing him of falsely testifying to Congress.
The new criminal complaint came to light hours after a federal judge in New York ruled that the Department of Justice had unlawfully fired Comey's daughter, Maurene Comey , last year as an assistant U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.
"Well, they're back — again," James Comey said in a video message on Substack addressing the new case.
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said. "Nothing's changed with me. I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
"And I'm still lucky to have an amazing family and an incredible group of lawyers that will stand up in court and fight the latest and whatever comes after this," Comey said. "The next couple of years are going to be hard for all of us. It's really important that we stand straight and keep the faith in America."
In the pending indictment in North Carolina, Comey in late April was charged with threatening Trump's life by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to form the numbers "86 47."
Prosecutors claim that the number "86" — which is often used in restaurants to indicate a menu item is no longer available — was code for suggesting someone kill Trump, who is the 47th U.S. president.
Comey has denied any wrongdoing in that case and is seeking to have the indictment tossed out by a judge.
Comey was first indicted in September 2025 by a federal grand jury in Virginia on charges of making a false statement and obstruction, in connection with testimony he gave before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Sept. 30, 2020.
Comey, in that testimony, denied authorizing another person at the FBI to serve as an anonymous source in news reports regarding an investigation of Hillary Clinton and her emails when she was the Democratic presidential nominee in 2016.
That first indictment was dismissed by a judge on Nov. 24, 2025, after the judge ruled that Lindsey Halligan, a then-interim U.S. attorney who obtained the indictments, had been invalidly appointed.
On the same day the judge tossed Comey's case for that reason, the same judge dismissed an unrelated indictment obtained by Halligan against New York Attorney General Letitia James, who had been accused of bank fraud and making false statements to a financial institution in connection with a home mortgage she obtained in 2020.
James, like Comey, has been a staunch critic of Trump, and a target of the president's ire.

articles.title_orig: Online post purportedly by Chinese students calls for restoring term limits for Xi
articles.title_zh: Online post purportedly by Chinese students calls for restoring term limits for Xi
articles.content_orig:
Read a version of this story in Chinese
An “open letter” purportedly signed by students from multiple Chinese universities appeared on a Chinese language website on Monday, calling for the restoration of term limits for the Chinese president, but an investigation by Radio Free Asia was not able to determine if it originated from within China.
The letter, which also called for the promotion of democratic constitutional amendments and the guarantee of space for citizens to discuss national affairs, appeared the same day as the opening of the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).
RFA’s investigation revealed that the “Siyuan Lake BBS” website hosting the message listed “KR” as its country/region code, indicating South Korea, in its registration information. Its mailing address was listed as “16 Collyer Quay,” a skyscraper in Singapore’s central business district. The administrator’s email address was registered on a server of Chinese tech giant Tencent.
Based on the above information, RFA was unable to determine whether the Chinese language website is located within China. As for which organization or company manages it, this cannot be verified at present.
The “open letter,” posted at 3:18 p.m., was titled “A Joint Appeal from a Group of University Students in the Republic.” It was addressed to the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China, the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress, and members of the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th CPC Central Committee, and was written against the backdrop of commemorating the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen, the founder of modern China at the end of its last imperial dynasty.
The article cites past statements by Sun Yat-sen, Mao Zedong, and Deng Xiaoping regarding democracy, oversight of power, and leadership systems, and questions China’s 2018 constitutional amendment that removed the two-term limit for the president and vice president. It argues that political stability should stem from predictability in the system and advocates for “limiting the time limit on power and subjecting it to oversight.”
The open letter put forward three main expectations:
Restore Term Limits: Abolish the indefinite extension of the term of office for the President of the People’s Republic of China and restore the term limits explicitly stipulated in the Constitution to ensure the orderly transfer of power; clear term limits should also be established for the highest leadership positions of the Party.
Initiate Democratic Constitutional Amendment: Convene a national constitutional amendment conference, steadily and gradually expand the people’s substantive participation in public power, improve the election, supervision, and recall mechanisms, and put into practice the unfinished goal since the 1911 Xinhai Revolution—returning power to the people—step by step.
Safeguard Space for Public Discussion: Safeguard the space for citizens to discuss national affairs in accordance with the law, encourage young people of the Republic to speak the truth, and listen to criticism as well-intentioned suggestions.
“We have no intention of confrontation, much less to create antagonism. We are just a group of young people who grew up reading Dr. Sun Yat-sen’s last words, and with the sentiment that ‘the revolution has not yet succeeded, comrades must continue to strive,’ we are willing to fulfill the responsibility of a scholar for the long-term future of this country.”
The post lists 14 universities, including Peking University, Renmin University of China, Tongji University, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xiamen University, and Nankai University, and notes that the petition is ongoing. However, the list only includes the names of the universities and does not provide any individual signatures or proof of signature.
As of midnight Beijing time on October 27, the website showed that this article had only been viewed by 656 people and received 1 like. The author on the page is listed as “Lin Ziyi,” with an account level of “LV.1.” The website indicates that this is “Lin Ziyi’s” first article. The article does not provide the names, number, contact information, or other verifiable information of the students who signed the article.
RFA has not independently confirmed the author’s identity, whether the signatories are indeed students, or whether students from the listed schools actually participated.
The website is divided into several topics, with the “Open Letter” posted in the “Complaints and Casual Chat” section. The website is entirely in simplified Chinese and appears to be a typical campus job search or lifestyle information website.
The bottom of the page states that it is a “non-official campus forum,” and a closer look reveals that its URL ends with “.com” instead of the usual “.cn” which is China’s internet domain.
Radio Free Asia further investigated the website’s registration information and found that the IP address used by the website was “43.155.168.161”. Further verification with ICANN revealed that the website’s registration information showed the “country/region” code as “KR”, which corresponds to South Korea. The mailing address was listed as “16 Collyer Quay” in Singapore, but the administrator’s email address was registered on a Tencent server (@tencent.com), and the mobile phone number and WeChat account left by the administrator were also Chinese numbers.
Edited by Charlie Dharapak.

articles.title_orig: Tesla stock leaves rest of the Magnificent 7 in the dust, surging to October’s top spot
articles.title_zh: Tesla stock leaves rest of the Magnificent 7 in the dust, surging to October’s top spot
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
For most of 2026, Tesla has been the Magnificent Seven's minivan. In October, it's the only one leaving skid marks.
Tesla ( TSLA ) stock jumped about 5% Monday, its best day since early September and its highest close in about three months. The rest of Big Tech was a mixed bag, with Apple ( AAPL ), Alphabet ( GOOGL ), and Meta ( META ) all ending lower.
That leaves Tesla with two very different report cards. It's still down by double digits this year, the worst showing in the Magnificent Seven. But it's up by double digits in October, the best in the group, while Meta, Alphabet, and Nvidia ( NVDA ) are all lower for the month.
The stock opened above Friday's high — a gap — and pushed through the $386 area. That level is both Tesla's highest close of October and roughly its 200-day moving average , a long-term trend line many traders watch. Clearing both at once is what makes this a breakout.
Even so, Tesla remains about a fifth below its record close.
The rally came alongside a Barclays upgrade betting that a Tesla merger with SpaceX ( SPCX ) would hand shareholders a takeout premium , as Pras Subramanian reported . Barclays raised its price target to $450 from $370. Musk confirmed last week that the two companies had formed independent committees to explore a combination, though no deal has been announced.
Tesla is already in on the joke. On Monday, its Robotaxi service switched on a bigger Houston service area shaped like a Starship rocket, announced with a "Houston, we have liftoff" post. "I swear it's just a coincidence 😂," Musk replied on X.
A combination wouldn't just bring rockets. On Sunday, Musk said SpaceX had closed $40 billion in debt financing to buy AI chips, and he also warned about neoclouds — rent-a-GPU cloud companies such as CoreWeave ( CRWV ) — as my colleague Ines Ferré reported . A merged company would share that chip bill.
Watch $386. Holding it keeps the liftoff on course, while a slide back below would turn Monday into a one-day pop. Above, the next stop is the low $450s, where Barclays' target and Tesla's 2026 closing high nearly overlap.

articles.title_orig: What Vucic’s defeat means for Serbia’s foreign policy
articles.title_zh: What Vucic’s defeat means for Serbia’s foreign policy
articles.content_orig:
Serbia has reached a watershed moment following 14 years of authoritarian rule by Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).
Sunday’s election delivered a historic victory for the opposition Student List, ending the political dominance that Vucic and the SNS had exercised/enforced for 14 years.
As Belgrade prepares for a turbulent transition and the upcoming presidential elections in December, international observers and regional neighbours have been asking whether Vucic’s departure will prompt a shift in Serbia’s foreign policy.
However, while international analysts often anticipate a quick foreign policy pivot toward the West whenever an authoritarian regime falls, experts warn that internal consolidation will take immediate priority and any transformation will be gradual.
Domestic cleanup before regional reset
SNS’s defeat has brought a mixture of cautious optimism and uncertainty across the Western Balkans. Serbia’s relations with Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Kosovo have often been frayed by Vucic’s nationalistic rhetoric.
Aleksandar Popov, director of the Centre for Regionalism in Novi Sad in Serbia, told Al Jazeera that a rapid reset in regional relations was unlikely.
“These questions will not be on the agenda immediately,” he said, referring to relations with Serbia’s neighbours.
The new authorities will first have to tackle domestic problems, he said, including dealing with a system that has “captured all democratic institutions”, as well as problems in the judiciary, prosecution service, police and media sector.
“Tidying up at home” will take priority before “solving problems with the neighbours”, Popov said, despite noting that the outgoing regime had done everything possible to undermine regional relations.
While relations with Croatia are “not frozen” neither are they “the way they should … be between neighbours”, being marked by frequent sharp words.
Amid recent mass protests in Serbia, Vucic accused Zagreb of organising a “colour revolution”.
In addition, “relations with Montenegro are disrupted and issues with Bosnia and Herzegovina remain unresolved,” he said.
Croatia is the thorniest case, Popov suggested, noting that relations deteriorated as the SNS clashed with Croatia’s ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), which stems from a similar nationalist-populist stable.
“Zagreb would fire a poisoned arrow at Serbia and that gave Belgrade an argument to retaliate,” he said, describing a system that “functioned on the production of internal and external enemies”.
Meanwhile, behind the public hostility, lay a quiet convergence on Bosnia and Herzegovina, he argued, with Belgrade backing Republika Srpska leader Milorad Dodik and Zagreb favouring a third entity.
He expressed hope that a new government in Serbia led by experts and civic leaders, would work towards stabilising the region and revive Serbia’s hopes of joining the European Union.
“The previous government sabotaged EU integration and the EU will not accept a country without good neighbourly relations. The new government’s task will be to repair those damaged ties,” Popov said.
Beyond the immediate neighbourhood, global powers are closely watching Belgrade.
Under Vucic, Serbia maintained a delicate balancing act, refusing to impose sanctions on Russia despite heavy pressure from the EU, while simultaneously allowing ammunition to flow indirectly to Ukraine.
Of all elements of Serbian public policy, foreign policy will transform the least under the forthcoming governmental changes, Vuk Vuksanovic, a lecturer in foreign policy at King’s College London, predicted to Al Jazeera.
“Many international and domestic structures that shape Serbian foreign policy will remain in place,” he said, adding that Moscow never fully trusted Vucic, but viewed him instead as “the devil they knew”.
Russian influence will take a blow, with the end of uncritical glorification of Moscow in Vucic-controlled tabloids and media and intelligence cooperation to be downgraded, he said, but the new government is unlikely to adopt a hawkish stance overnight.
Serbian interests can continue to be served by ties with Russia, he asserted. “The country still needs preferential gas prices, the Kosovo dispute remains unresolved and parts of the public remain disillusioned with the West.”
“The new Serbian government will not see value in joining EU sanctions or adopting a hawkish stance toward Moscow,” Vuksanovic continued.
“Regarding Ukraine, Serbia will maintain its policy of not recognising the annexation of Crimea and Donbas. However, there is a question mark over ammunition deliveries, as the opposition viewed Vucic’s weapons sales to Kyiv as a cynical ploy to buy Western tolerance for his domestic rule.”
Another critical dimension of Serbia’s external relations is its close relationship with Israel. Under Vucic, Serbia established a strong partnership with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, marked by arms trade and technology exchanges.
Bosko Jaksic, a foreign policy analyst, told Al Jazeera that while ties will not be severed, recent controversial agreements will face scrutiny.
“The new government has no reason to abandon cooperation with Israel, but it will certainly re-examine newly concluded contracts – primarily those concerning Serbian ammunition exports to Israel and Israeli surveillance equipment exports to Serbia,” Jaksic said.
The analyst also noted that Netanyahu’s government has lost another “authoritarian, nationalist ally” in Europe after Viktor Orban’s removal in Hungary earlier this year. However, Serbia’s future stance will also depend on political developments in Jerusalem.
“How Israel positions itself toward the new authorities in Belgrade depends largely on the outcome of Israel’s own elections,” Jaksic added.
Looking at the broader geopolitical alignment, he emphasised that Serbia’s foreign policy will inevitably undergo a review.
He suggested that “the policy of ‘sitting on multiple chairs,’ which brought Serbia more harm than good, will certainly be re-evaluated”, and that it is realistic to expect Belgrade to strengthen ties with the EU.
But as Serbia enters a new political era, the international community should expect a period of intense internal reform rather than sudden geopolitical realignments, all of the analysts agree.

articles.title_orig: United flight returns to airport after passenger spotted texting about hijacking aircraft
articles.title_zh: United flight returns to airport after passenger spotted texting about hijacking aircraft
articles.content_orig:
A United Airlines flight from Las Vegas to Newark returned to Harry Reid Airport on Saturday after a crew member spotted a passenger sending text messages saying he intended to hijack the aircraft, according to the online aviation publication Simple Flying.
The report cited air traffic control (ATC) recordings shared on X/Twitter showing the passenger was unaware of the emergency return to the airport, where law enforcement was waiting for him.
The pilot of United flight 1681, operated by a Boeing 737 MAX 8, can be heard in the recording saying that the cockpit went into "lockdown" following the report from the flight attendant about the threat, which Simple Flying reported occured shortly after departure.
The incident comes less than a month after the October 1 attempted hijacking of flydubai Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv by one of the pilots, Omani national Hamam al Hamami, who repeatedly struck the captain with an axe before being subdued by several Israeli passengers on board.
On Wednesday, the Transportation Ministry notified United that it had barred entry to Israel for one of its pilots over his Iran sympathies as the country tightens its foreign crew background check measures following the flydubai incident.
Regarding Saturday's incident, Simple Flying noted that the United aircraft's squawk code changed to 7700, signaling a general emergency, before it diverted. This differs from the hijack code, which is 7500.
In addition, the flight's return required a longer-than-standard route to burn off excess fuel, as the MAX 8 lacks fuel-dump capability and had tanks filled for its intended flight to Newark Liberty Airport, resulting in an overweight condition for an early landing.
As an added precaution, the pilot advised ATC that they may need the entirety of Runway 26L to land safely even after burning fuel, according to Simple Flying.
According to the published FAA airport diagram, Harry Reid Airport's Runway 26L is 10,526 feet (3,208 meters) long, more than 2,000 feet (610 meters) longer than the maximum landing distance listed in the aircraft's official performance charts, even with maximum weight and wet runway conditions.
It was not immediately clear why the pilot did not select parallel Runway 26R, which the diagram shows as nearly 4,000 feet (1,219 meters) longer than 26L, for added redundancy.
The aircraft landed safely despite the weight issues, according to Fox 5 Las Vegas, with no injuries reported among its 150 passengers and six crew members.
The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said in a preliminary statement that it intends to investigate the incident, and United told Fox 5 that the flight departed for Newark again on Sunday following the "potential security concern."
Fox 5 reached out to the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department for comment, but it did not respond at the time of writing.
Udi Etzion and Amit Avitan contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Shock Lula Win Derails $6 Billion in Equity Sales as Banks Reel
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Brazilian markets took a battering Monday following the shock reelection of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, but elsewhere investors were focused on artificial intelligence (AI) technology companies.
Lula came from behind to win in the second-round vote, but his right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro, has vowed to challenge the result.
Brazilian markets reeled as trading got under way, but pared some of the steepest losses by the close. The Sao Paulo stock exchange plummeted by 13.7 percent to near a two-month low, with the real down around 8.5 percent against the dollar.
"Instead of fiscal consolidation under Bolsonaro, Brazilian assets are instead going to have to contend with Lula's campaign pledges, including a shorter working week," said Chris Turner at ING bank.
Elsewhere, investors geared up for the week's crucial run of central bank decisions and tech earnings for major companies.
"The AI complex remains under a microscope ahead of what may be the most important stretch of earnings season so far," noted SPI Asset Management's Stephen Innes.
"Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are about to walk on stage, and this is not one of those quarters where a company can simply beat the number, raise the guidance by a whisker and expect applause. Investors want proof now.
"They want to know whether the billions going into the compute buildout are building a durable earnings machine or just a shinier version of the same old capex furnace," Innes added.
This week also sees the release of earnings from South Korean chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung.
- Testing investor appetite -
Results from Tesla and Meta last week stoked spending worries that weighed on stock markets.
Nevertheless, Meta announced Monday it was launching a stock offering that aims to raise $35 billion to fund its AI ambitions.
The parent company of Facebook and Instagram also announced plans to launch an additional stock offering of up to $60 billion, at a date yet to be determined.
Meta's shares fell by 1.88 percent at the close.
Anthropic, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence companies, on Monday made public its plans to sell shares on the stock market in mid-November.
The company reported first-half revenue up about 1,300 percent year-over-year, but also flagged safety risks.
Wall Street's main indices closed higher on Monday, with the tech-rich Nasdaq gaining 0.8 percent.
"Tech is once again mounting an attempt to rally, like a battered prize fighter getting up off the floor," said Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at online trading and investing platform IG.
"This bounce will be sorely tested in the days to come," he added.
Jose Torres of Interactive Brokers said investors were "embracing risk."
"Participants are reflecting a shift in demeanor regarding tech and AI, with recent turbulence offering bulls opportunities to raise exposures at cheaper prices," he said.
Europe's main indices closed higher, and Asia ended mixed after starting the day on the back foot following Friday's losses on Wall Street.
Oil prices hung around six-month highs amid supply concerns heading into the Northern Hemisphere winter.
"Rising oil prices are the kryptonite to any sustained rally in risk assets," said IG's Beauchamp.
Also in view this week are monetary policy decisions from the US Federal Reserve, European Central Bank (ECB) and Bank of Japan (BoJ), which are expected to hold rates steady.
The Bank of England is widely expected to hike in November after a jump in UK inflation ahead of the country's annual budget announcement due Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: Report: Silent Hill 1 Remake Targeting 2027 Release, First Cast Details Revealed
articles.title_zh: Report: Silent Hill 1 Remake Targeting 2027 Release, First Cast Details Revealed
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump apepars at a rally at Alico Arena on the Florida Gulf Coast University campus on Oct. 23, 2026, in Fort Myers, Florida.
A woman who had accused President Donald Trump of sexually assaulting her in 1993 described it to congressional staff as rape and said the interaction left her bleeding and bruised, according to a report released Monday by Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee examining Trump's ties to Jeffrey Epstein.
Beatrice Keul, a model and former Miss Switzerland, alleged to Judiciary Committee staff that she was raped by Trump in a Plaza Hotel suite in Manhattan when she was 24. Keul said that while attending the American Dream Pageant, which had a partnership with Trump, she met with Trump at a press luncheon at the event.
Trump, according to Keul, promised to arrange her visa in the U.S. and ensure her acceptance into New York University through his friend Paolo Zampolli, a close Trump ally who was, until earlier this month, part of his Administration. At the same event, she also spent at least 10 minutes talking to Epstein who she said claimed to have organized “many parties with Don.”
Later that day, Keul alleges, Trump invited her to a hotel suite where Trump “grabbed Keul from behind and forcibly raped her,” causing “bleeding and bruising on multiple parts of her body,” the report says. Following the incident, Keul alleges Trump made her promise she would keep quiet and repeated his promise for visa and college admission.
Because Keul’s passport had been taken from her on her arrival, she was not able to leave the contest following the incident, she alleges, according to the report. After she returned to Switzerland, she declined to participate in an additional Trump-sponsored pageant in Hawaii several weeks later.
TIME has been unable to independently verify details of Keul’s account.
In a statement, the White House denies the allegations and says that President Trump has been “fully exonerated of anything related to Epstein.” “This ‘report’ is nothing more than a desperate attempt by crazed Democrats to distract Americans from the surging Republican momentum driven by President Trump’s historic achievements,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis says.
Keul has previously spoken in public about her sexual assault allegations against Trump, but the report provided new details of the alleged rape—as well as reviewing similar accounts of other Trump accusers.
Read more: Trump Said He Banned Epstein From Mar-a-Lago. A Lawmaker Who Reviewed Unredacted Files Says They Tell a Different Story
In addition to Keul’s account, the report also compiled allegations from four other women who have directly accused Trump of rape or sexual assault in connection with the Epstein investigation. The allegations, spanning from the mid-1980s to the 1990s, had all been previously made public either through media interviews or FBI testimony released as part of the Epstein files.
The report’s release, just over a week before Election Day, comes as Democrats are working to signal to voters how they will make use of their power if they gain control of one or both chambers of Congress.
On Monday, Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat of the House Judiciary Committee, called on the Department of Justice to appoint an independent special counsel to oversee the investigation of allegations mentioned in the report. So far, Ghislaine Maxwell , a longtime Epstein confidant, is the only person to have been convicted of sex trafficking of minors in connection with the Epstein case.
“An independent special counsel must investigate Epstein’s co-conspirators and DOJ’s cover-up and ensure that state and foreign prosecutors have the evidence they need to pursue justice,” Raskin said in a statement.
The report also alleges that Zampolli, a former Trump administration official and a close Trump ally, was “an active participant” in the Epstein sex trafficking allegations.
According to the report, which cites multiple FBI reports included in the Epstein files, Zampolli arranged U.S. visas for young female models before they met Epstein. One FBI report mentioned that Zampolli arranged an 18-year-old model’s visa before she was recruited to give a massage at Epstein’s house, where Epstein allegedly raped her.
Zampolli himself has also been accused of rape and sexual assault in a separate case brought by model Victoria Drake, who alleges in an ongoing civil lawsuit that Zampolli drugged and raped her in 2023.
TIME has reached out to Zampolli for comment.
Previously, Zampolli has claimed that he had introduced First Lady Melania Trump to the President in 1998, but the report disputes that claim, citing two accounts—one from an unnamed Epstein associate and the other from Amanda Ungaro, a Brazilian model—saying that Epstein had introduced Melania Trump to Donald Trump.
The New York Times reported in March that Zampolli had asked a top official at Immigration and Customs Enforcement  last year to detain and deport Ungaro, whom Zampolli had previously dated, amid a custody battle over their son. Zampolli denied making such requests.
Until earlier this month, Zampolli held a diplomatic role under the State Department as Special Representative for Global Partnerships. He was fired two weeks ago over a months-long dispute with the department’s deputy secretary, according to Politico .

articles.title_orig: One supply scare pushed China into renewables. Two real crises still haven’t woken Europe up
articles.title_zh: One supply scare pushed China into renewables. Two real crises still haven’t woken Europe up
articles.content_orig:
In 2003, Chinese president Hu Jintao worried about what became known among the country’s leadership as the ‘Malacca dilemma.’
Some 80 percent of China’s imported crude passed through the Malacca strait which Beijing’s naval forces could not control.
This gave rise to a wider security doctrine of supply-chain resilience which became the basis for China’s transformation into the clean tech powerhouse it is today.
When the US–Iran war disrupted Middle Eastern oil flows this year, Xi Jinping called China’s early bet on wind and solar “forward-looking” – as recounted in a new paper from the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute published on Monday (26 October).
The paper identifies green growth as “the answer” to geopolitical uncertainty. Clean tech isn’t just clean, it’s also secure and not dependent on imports. Plus, it delivers a “more durable pathway” to “economic resilience.”
Some governments want to expand fossil-fuel imports, or drill more oil or gas wells, arguing that a more diversified supply chain improves resilience. But the paper dismissed that.
Oil and gas are priced on global markets, so even producers are exposed to price shocks. More North Sea drilling would save UK households between £16 and £82 (€19 to €98) a year, the paper finds, citing Oxford University research, compared with £105 to £441 on a renewables and electrification pathway.
It's interesting comparing how the two political systems respond to (hypothetical) supply shocks. In China, the mere threat of losing control of one strait was enough to transform energy politics gradually over many years.
